speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity pursuant to the provisions of Standing Order 43. In view of unprecedented unemployment and general economic deterioration across the country, centred in the Atlantic provinces, and the need for labour intensive projects which will provide lasting benefits, particularly to the primary sector, I move, seconded by the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Howie):

Mr. Speaker, I rise for the purpose of proposing a motion under Standing Order 26 regarding a very serious matter. Without making reference to that aspect of the application of which the Chair had notice from the hon. member as required by the Standing Orders regarding the discussion or the disagreement as to whether unemployment changes from continuing or chronic to crisis proportions as a result of the release of the figures, I have to adjudicate the matter on the basis of Standing Order 26(5), which reads as follows:
In determining whether a matter should have urgent consideration, Mr. Speaker shall have regard to the extent to which it concerns the administrative responsibilities of the government or could come within the scope of ministerial action-
These are the operative words.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to take this opportunity to make a few remarks on behalf of my constituents, the people of the Northwest Territories, in this budget debate. I suppose in a way I am breaking a tradition which has long been held by members of the opposition in replying to major government policy statements when 1 stand here representing the people of the Northwest Territories and say that I am in agreement with at least part of the minister's budget. When the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) delivered his budget address, those of us who listened carefully found an almost constant message running throughout the budget. Hidden in the little explanatory remarks in the speech was the message that the Canadian economy was in pretty poor shape.
I would like to take this opportunity to say that for once I support the minister's claim and wholeheartedly agree with him that the economy is in poor shape. I can also report to the minister that many people are unemployed and many Canadi-

April 18, 1977
The Budget-Mr. Firth
ans are suffering. People who live on fixed incomes, Canadians who earn low incomes and even Canadians who earn not so low incomes would agree with the minister that the Canadian economy is indeed in pretty poor shape. It is a tribute to the minister and to his government that so many people agree with his assessment of something this government has managed to do.
However, that is where my agreement with the budget ends. This budget comes at a particularly important time in Canadian history. It comes at a time when all Canadians, perhaps for the first time in generations, are assessing the role of the federal government. All Canadians are wondering about the nature of confederation. Many Canadians are asking themselves what should be the relationship between their particular regions and the federal government. I had hoped that the minister would have been a little more sensitive to these kinds of questions as he was preparing the budget. I had hoped that the minister would have taken into consideration the fact that Canada is a diverse country with many different regional problems requiring different solutions. Many agree with this, and that is true in the north. We have to look at northern problems and find northern solutions.
I had hoped that the minister would not have fallen into the trap of proposing catch-all solutions which catch all the problems of some of the people in central Canada but which leave the rest of the country working with a budget which just does not fit. I suppose I had hoped for too much. While Canadians have been trying to decide how to put their regional differences together to form a stronger confederation, this minister has the insensitivity to come up with a budget which barely acknowledges any regional differences at all. At least the minister and this government are being consistent in that respect. Instead of providing proof that this government can come up with workable solutions which will bind Canadians closer together, the Minister of Finance seems to have fallen back on the tried and true solution of giving concessions to the Toronto business community in the hope that it will come through with magical jobs and investment. I believe we have tried that one for too many years and it just does not work.
We northern people had hoped that the minister would pay a little attention to some of the unique conditions which rule the economy of the Northwest Territories. This budget did not touch on one of those things we desperately need in the north, things we must have if we are to continue to decolonize the economy of the Northwest Territories en route to full provincial status. I am speaking, of course, of a little bit of stability. After years of bungling there is now such a mess in the area of government planning and policy-making for the north that it is no wonder the economy of the Northwest Territories suffers.
It is no wonder that business operators in the north are hesitant about investing any more money or creating any more jobs. We are now faced with a situation where people simply do not know what foolish move the government will adopt next. What we northerners want and need is a federal government which will set out and stick with policies which will create a stable situation in which the many people who are

making decisions in the economy feel comfortable forecasting beyond the next 20 minutes or half hour.
Part of the stability we need can only be found in increased control over local government. How can local business and industry be expected to flourish when all the important decisions are made thousands of miles away in places such as Ottawa, New York and Chicago? Despite all the government's words to the contrary, we have been moving backward in this respect. For example, as recently as three weeks ago a workshop on local government was to be held to promote self-government in the Northwest Territories. It was to be a workshop on how to deal with the details of local government, everything from how to fix plumbing to how to fill out forms, how to apply for licences, and so forth.
That conference was called off and reinstated twice by the Commissioner of the Northwest Territories. The "off again-on again" tactics of the government of the Northwest Territories so frustrated the organizers of the workshop that they were forced to cancel it altogether. That workshop was to be held at Baker Lake, Northwest Territories. The organizers were forced to cancel the workshop when most of the delegates were already making their way there. That was a waste of time and money for many people, and it was extremely frustrating. Why was the Commissioner so worried that he twice refused permission for the workshop to be held? He was worried because several paragraphs of a 50-page background paper made reference to the use of radical tactics when dealing with senior levels of government.
In his wisdom, the Commissioner decided that northern people should not be exposed to the works of the late Saul Alinsky. Northern people were not allowed to hear of a man whose books on politics are available to any high school student who cares to read them, a man whom the National Film Board considered important enough to be the subject of a documentary film. How are we to develop northern resources to create a strong community when the official responsible for that development treats us as naughty children? How are we to cope with the economic side of development when the Minister of Finance does not even acknowledge that we exist?
Let us consider housing which I have mentioned in this House, in committee and other places across Canada. The minister made several references in his budget-all glowing- to the great increase in the number of houses built during the past year. Taken by themselves, the minister's figures for housing construction look impressive in our stagnant economy, but in the part of the country that I represent-and, I am sure, in many other parts as well-the figures do not match the real world. I am sure many members of the House would agree that a decent place to live in is a basic human right. Many people in the Northwest Territories are denied that right.
In some communities the government has introduced prefabricated housing, houses that fall apart after a few of our northern winters. In some communities, services for the houses we have are non-existent, which means that people still have to
April 18, 1977

melt snow and ice in order to get water for drinking, cooking and laundry. The shortage and poor quality of the houses in the north is a factor in every social problem that exists there, from public health to alcoholism. To put it in terms the minister may feel more comfortable with, these social problems cost the government a great deal of money each year. If the minister had tried to do something about the housing shortage, he would have been able to save a great deal in his account for child welfare and other programs, while at the same time providing jobs and incomes for a number of workers in my constituency.
1 referred earlier to the federal government treating northern Canada as a kind of colony. The housing policy of the federal government is a good example of this. In most northern communities, particularly in the eastern Arctic, only public housing is available. People have no opportunity to own their own home and the public housing is often inadequate for their needs. These northern residents have to pay at least 25 per cent of their income-which is usually very low and in some cases non-existent-for this inadequate housing. This is a severe hardship for many. On the other hand, federal and territorial government employees are provided with heavily subsidized housing of superior quality which, of course, has all the necessary facilities.
For several years 1 have asked the government to start a log housing program in the north. This could be started tomorrow morning, and should have been started many years ago, especially in the Mackenzie district of the Northwest Territories. I believe this program would provide an essential service to the north. We would make houses from an indigenous, renewable natural resource, rather than importing material from other regions of Canada. Residents would be employed in meeting their housing needs, instead of virtually all the jobs in the industry going to other regions. The communities of the north would have an opportunity to control their housing policy and decide their needs.
This idea of northern control over basic human necessities such as housing is very important for regional dignity, but I see no such concept in the budget. Indeed, there is not very much in the budget for small business operators, especially those in the north. The small business community in Canada is large. It provides a great percentage of jobs in southern Canada, and the proceeds stay there. Of course, a healthy economy needs small business. In the north, the small business community forms only a very small part of the economy and is kept in that position because it must operate under conditions which simply do not allow it to grow.
For over two years small business operators in the north have tried to get the government to listen to their problems and make simple but important changes-changes which would bring them opportunities in line with those readily available to their counterparts in southern Canada. Not very long ago, in July, 1975, a task force on northern business published its report and listed some 42 measures that the federal and territorial governments should follow in order to create a better climate for small business in the north. After
The Budget-Mr. Firth
two years of review and several promises of a new code of treatment for small business operators in the north, we find that very little has happened.
Just before the Easter recess I raised a question on this matter in the House. It was interesting that the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Allmand) said that he agreed with the recommendations of the task force but was having difficulty in getting his colleagues to accept them. Not long ago I received a letter from the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) which indicated that he does not seem to agree.
Another thing that really hurts us in the north is prices. My friends and I have spent a great deal of time telling the government that their anti-inflation program does not work, and now it seems that even the Anti-Inflation Board agrees and has released figures to this effect. The figures show that consumers in southern Canada have been badly hit in the pocket. In the Toronto area, as the Minister of Finance should know, the cost of a good diet for a family of four, for one week, went from an estimated $42.42 in March, 1976, to $46.15 in March, 1977-an increase of $3.73 in one year. In my part of the country the price of the same basket of food in the same period went from $56.60 to $63.43. Just the price of food alone should open the eyes of many of the ministers across the way, but it does not seem to make any impression on them at all. It does not seem to me that there is anything in this budget to help reduce that kind of regional difference.
I should also like to comment on the government's attempt at job creation, Mr. Speaker. The Canada Works Program for all of Canada was allocated $110 million for phase one. Of this amount, $1.5 million, or 1 per cent, was allocated to the Northwest Territories. That may sound like a lot of money, but it is only a drop in the bucket as far as meeting the real needs of northern residents is concerned. This program does absolutely nothing for those who most need it, for those who do not read and write, for people who may not even be aware of the existence of such programs. They are not capable of going down to the Manpower offices even if there were an office within 2,000 or 3,000 miles of the village; therefore, the program meets only in a small way the employment needs of northern residents.
As far as I can see, northern residents have been left out of this budget. I suspect that many people in other regions of the country have also been excluded because, apparently, the minister and his colleagues refuse to acknowledge that we have in this country economic problems different from those of central Canada. It is about time the government recognized these regional differences. Let it correct those differences if it wants to do something of benefit for all Canada. Mr. Speaker, in this wonderful, rich country of ours, I suggest that good housing for all Canadians, no matter where they may live, is a basic human right. The government so ought to consider it.

speechtext:
I now wish to comment on the proposed pipeline which will transport gas down the Mackenzie Valley. Apparently the need for such a pipeline has been accepted by many people, and I think a decision about it is pending. I believe the Berger report will soon be handed down, as will the National Energy Board report and other reports. Unfortunately, an idea which I think makes sense has not been considered by many of the people responsible for making such decisions.
Mr. Speaker, many in this House know that my platform in two federal elections in the Northwest Territories was this: no pipelines or major projects should be started in the Northwest Territories until native claims have been settled. Let us suppose for a moment that such claims had been settled and it had been agreed that for the good of all Canadians we must build a system for moving oil and gas from the north to southern markets. So far many people have accepted the idea of a pipeline. Unfortunately, the idea of building a railway to move such resources was not given a fair chance. I firmly believe that if the railway companies and those who support the use of railways for moving resources such as natural gas and oil from the north had been given the same opportunity as the oil companies for making their case, the authorities would have preferred a railway to a pipeline.
It has been proven that railways work well in northern areas. There is a railway in Alaska and one in the Yukon. The White Pass Railway has been doing a good job for many years. There is a railway serving the Moosonee area of Canada and a rail line to Churchill, Manitoba, which traverses muskeg and difficult country. There is already a railway in the Northwest Territories extending for half the distance the proposed pipeline would run if it were decided to build a pipeline. I think using a railway makes good economic sense. For obvious reasons it is the course of common sense.
A well developed transportation system in the Liard River area of northern Canada would open up tremendous possibilities in agriculture. I know that many in the south think the north is frozen all year, or for many months, and that it is very difficult to grow potatoes, cabbage, wheat or other crops. But it has been shown time and again by many individuals that the agricultural possibilities of the Mackenzie area are enormous. I, personally, have seen some fantastically large cabbages, turnips and other basic vegetables which have come from that area. One can grow good crops in the north. For example, a chap by the name of McBride, I think, in the Hay River area not far from the Alberta border decided one day to grow rapeseed. The government's agricultural experts told him that the rapeseed plant cannot grow in the north. He ignored them, went ahead and planted rapeseed, and when he brought it to the elevator operators they said it was among the best rapeseed they had ever seen. He grew the crop despite the opinion of government experts who said it could not be grown in the north.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That seems to be the government's attitude in many matters.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I agree with the statement of the Minister of Finance that the economy of this country is in deep trouble. But that is about the only statement in the budget with which I agree. I disagree with all the rest of the budget. I will not take up any more time of the House. Let me say, simply, that I appreciate this opportunity to express my views on what should have been excluded from the budget and what should have been included.

speakerposition: Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before I speak on the Budget let me make some comments about two events which took place in the House before the resumption of this debate, after the Easter recess. The first was a motion brought forward by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) that the House do now adjourn. I gather the primary reason for that motion was the absence from the House of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) who is now in Winnipeg and is to make a speech on national unity tonight in an important forum. The opposition, by moving that motion, seemed to
April 18, 1977

imply that if the Prime Minister is not physically present in the House, this House ought to adjourn.
True, we appreciate that high compliment paid to the Prime Minister of Canada. He is a most important figure, of course, and he exerts a central influence in the chamber, but I do not think his presence in the House is essential if the House is to meet. I do not think the Prime Minister would expect the opposition to pay him that kind of compliment. You can imagine the hue and cry which would have gone up from the opposition if before the Easter recess the Prime Minister had said that because he would be away this Monday to deliver a speech, and because he felt the opposition were incompetent and could not function without his presence in the House, the House should not meet. Surely that would have been considered as the height of arrogance.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Right on.

speakerposition: Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And I think it would have been.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Right on.

speakerposition: Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I find it strange that the opposition think the House should not sit because the Prime Minister is absent doing something in terms of national unity. I find something else difficult to comprehend. From time to time, directly and indirectly, the opposition has said that the Prime Minister and the government of Canada ought to do more to encourage national unity, or that they should not sit back on their haunches but should do something positive. The Prime Minister is doing something positive in Winnipeg. Opposition members seem to feel he should not be there to talk to the Canadian people. This brings me to the other motion that I also find difficult to comprehend.
The right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) moved a motion proposing to censure the government because the Prime Minister and other ministers dared to make speeches and announcements outside this chamber which the opposition felt ought to be made in the chamber. It is evident that parliament is here to serve the people, not to be served by the people. It is equally evident that one of the purposes of government is to communicate with the people.
For parliament to usurp unto itself the exclusive prerogative of hearing everything directly for the first time would be asking it to stand as an intermediary between the Prime Minister, and the people's government and themselves. That is not the meaning of parliament. We should certainly insist on parliament being informed of what is happening; however, it does not follow that government should not communicate directly with the people of this country on important national issues, particularly with regard to national unity.
A third event occurred during the recess which concerned me. In a letter to the president of the CBC, the Leader of the Opposition complained about the media covering the speech of the Prime Minister in Winnipeg either fully or in large part. That is very disturbing. I find it inconceivable that any party
The Budget-Mr. Cafik
would think it unfair or inappropriate that the remarks of a prime minister of any country or leader of any nation should be denied to the people of that nation. Surely it is fundamental that a prime minister of whatever political stripe ought to communicate with the people so they may know directly his views and thoughts on such a central issue as national unity.
The action taken by the Leader of the Opposition illustrates a partisanship that is counterproductive to the interests of this country and holding it together. Frankly, this nation suffers far too much from over zealous partisan activity on the part of many of us.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Read the letter.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It has been suggested that I read the letter. To my knowledge that letter has not been fully made public. I have not been able to find a copy of it. If someone, when speaking in this debate wants to read the letter, I would be happy to hear its precise contents.
I gather that one of the central points of the letter is that the Leader of the Opposition wants equal time. I find that extraordinary even from a partisan standpoint. The opposition seems to think that everything the Prime Minister does is counterproductive. If that were true and they believed it, they would be delighted to give him all the exposure he could get in order to prove their point. The fact is they know that when the Prime Minister makes a speech on such an important subject it is such a moving speech that it has great meaning to the Canadian people. They just do not want that to happen.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Now that I have become carried away on this particular tack, there is one other comment I cannot resist making. The principle of freedom of information has been espoused by a great many members. It is supported on all sides of the House. I agree with the principle that government ought to operate with as little secrecy as possible; that is a fine principle. However, it is rather amusing for the official opposition to advocate such a marvellous stance because they think there will be some political advantage to them, and then in recent days turn around and have the Leader of the Opposition impose a kind of cabinet solidarity on a cabinet that does not even exist. If he feels that freedom of information and an exchange of ideas is healthy for a government, he should know that it is even more healthy for an opposition to practice. However, now that they are muzzling their own members they will have to reconsider the sacred principle of freedom of information except in so far as it applies to the government rather than to themselves.
Turning my thoughts to the budget, I will make a few brief comments. First, there has been a lot of criticism of the budget by opposition members, but very little criticism of any sustained or meaningful nature from the public at large. The business community recognizes that it has a responsibility to assist in creating employment. The government recognizes it has to provide tax measures and incentives to assist them in doing that in order to help the unemployed of this country. In

April 18, 1977
The Budget-Mr. Cafik
so far as the business community is concerned, this budget deals with unemployment it in a very precise manner. It gives concessions to them which immediately will be translated into job creation in this country. That is a very responsible role.
In terms of stimulating the purchasing power of Canadians through personal tax cuts, it is exclusively geared to those in the lower income brackets who really need the assistance. The tax cuts involved in the immediate budget proposals are in the neighbourhood of $500 million. Add to that the tax cut inherent in the escalation of exemptions that took place at the beginning of the year, which was another $950 million, and the job creation incentives for industry, and you have economic measures for this year which total close to $2.5 billion.
In a time of restraint and cutting back of government expenditures we really cannot expect much more than has been done in this budget to stimulate purchasing power and create jobs. One, of course, is fully aware of the moneys that have been put into the Canada Works and Young Canada Works programs. I believe that the figure for Canada Works, with the increase, is now $110 million. This is geared primarily to those areas of highest unemployment. Those of us from areas of considerably lower unemployment are very happy to see that incentive skewed in that particular direction.
Initially, the Young Canada Works program was to have $20 million for job creation for our young people. An additional $30 million was added to that amount, making $50 million. This gives us a gross figure for job creation not far off $200 million. There is no question that that amount, significant as it is, will not create full employment in Canada. We cannot find enough jobs for all the unemployed through that kind of measure. If we are substantively to correct the unemployment problem we must work very closely with the private sector to create the job opportunities that will be required in this country within the next ten years.
The high unemployment rate that we hear so much about today has to be put in some kind of perspective. Aside from Mexico, Canada has the greatest increase in the number of people seeking new jobs each year of any country in the world. We are creating an enormous number of good jobs every year, but because of the rapid rise in our population we are going through a period in which it is extremely difficult to keep pace with job formation at the rate which is required.
The government cannot buy itself out of this situation, given our present deficit position. Efforts to do so would in any case be in the nature of a band-aid approach. Thus, as a long-term solution we have to encourage the private sector to provide jobs. Also, at all times we must balance our concern for unemployment against our program to control inflation. It goes without saying that a high rate of inflation in Canada, one which exceeds that of our trading partners, is counter-productive in terms of exports. Canada is the largest exporting nation, per capita, of any in the world. It is all the more necessary, then, that our fight against inflation should be a success. The program has already scored significant successes
[Mr. Cafik.)
in the first 18 months of its existence and it must continue this record, otherwise we shall find ourselves priced completely out of the international market which in turn would result in worsening employment prospects.
Another important element in this picture is the value of the Canadian dollar. I recall a conversation in my office with a lawyer from a Toronto firm. After conducting business on another matter we began discussing the general economic situation, and this lawyer-I presume he is knowledgeable about a wide range of subjects-expressed concern about the point at which the Canadian dollar would settle in relation to other currencies. Would it go down to 90 cents, for example, or to 85 cents in relation to the U.S. dollar, and what would be the effect on job creation? I suggested that my visitor was not taking all the factors into consideration. There can be no question that the lower level of the Canadian dollar implies certain hidden benefits in terms of job creation. When the Canadian dollar is low, let us say that the level is 90 cents, we are evidently getting a 10 per cent advantage in terms of exporting our products. This results in more jobs becoming available in Canada and assists us in fighting inflation.
There is another impact which could also have positive benefits. Consider the question of imports coming into a country whose dollar has been devalued. In some ways the impact is adverse, but there is no question that increasing the cost of importing goods provides more opportunity for Canadian producers to manufacture goods for sale at home. For example, those who might normally import parts from the United States and elsewhere are encouraged to produce those parts at home because the cost of importing them is greater, reflecting the lower value of our dollar. Each of these elements can have a positive impact upon job creation. As I say, there are some adverse effects resulting from the lowered value of the Canadian dollar, but I am not at all sure they offset the benefits to which I have referred.
Moving away from the budget itself I should like to make a few comments about specific areas with which we ought to be concerned. First of all, I believe far too many people in our society look upon every group other than our own with a jaundiced eye. They think they are being ripped off by the business community, or by labour, or by big business, or by politicians, or whatever. There is continual tension between divergent groups-labour and management, French speaking and English speaking, politicians and constituents. It seems to me that at a time when we face a problem of national unity, at a time when we are trying to create a basis of understanding and co-operation between all these various groups in our society, it is important that all of us in positions of responsibility should act in such a way as to avoid fanning the flames of disunity.
All of us, as private members of parliament, as members of political parties, must work together in an unusually co-operative way in order to reach a common objective. With this in mind, we ought to be prepared to set aside our own political concerns in order to achieve something which is so greatly in the public interest. In other words, we must attempt to create
April 18, 1977

an understanding within our constituencies that self-interest is best served by attending to the common good of all the various interests in society. In other words, we might consider taking the beam out of our own eyes rather than calling attention to the mote in someone else's-a practice at which many of us are adept.

speakerposition: Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In any event, the hon. member is pregnant with contradiction. One can see that at every turn. Although I like him very much and generally get along with him very well in the finance committee, I must say that his contradictions are more notable than the areas in which he happens to agree with himself.
There are other subjects I wish to talk about. I mentioned one in a speech the other day in the House of Commons. I certainly hope the government will give serious consideration, when reviewing its programs, to providing more loan capital and perhaps even equity capital for small business ventures. I hope, also, that efforts in this field will be geared to job creation. I have always found it disturbing that when someone needs assistance from the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, and they get carried away and say, "We can create new jobs", the departmental officials say, "That is fine, but it is not relevant to this program". The fact of the matter is that we are now facing a very serious level of unemployment, so I think they ought to plan their programs to take more into account, job creation, job maintenance and export opportunities, and to do so by way of loan or equity capital rather than in the way they are proceeding now.
Secondly in that area I should like to see something done to assist our small business community and others develop export markets abroad. We are taking steps in this direction, and I welcome all of them, some of which are very effective. But frankly, I believe that we should have a federal export trading company with specific responsibility in this area. We ought to take a leaf out of the book of some very successful economies, such as those of Japan and Germany, which really use this technique with significant benefit to the working population within those countries. Certainly I hope we will do more than we have in the past.
The Budget-Mr. Cafik
Another area where we need a little further effort is in matching job skills to job opportunities. There is no question that the Department of Manpower and Immigration, through many of its job creation programs-the on the job program is a good one-and through their community college job training and upgrading of skills programs, provide some pretty good training opportunities. However, I sometimes wonder about their efficiency. I recall having a meeting with community college officials regarding these Manpower training programs and I discovered, much to my amazement, something that concerned me very greatly, namely, that if a person with very limited academic training wanted to become a welder and had a grade eight education, he had to upgrade his education to grade 11 or grade 12 or perhaps go right through high school before he ever saw a welding machine; and of course the program only lasted one or two years, so such a person started a welding course and all he got out of it was a grade nine education.
It seems to me that far too much emphasis is put on academic qualifications in programs that upgrade skills. I think we must do more to develop specific skills in a crash program. I just do not believe that you have to have a university education, or even a high school education, to become a welder or tool and die maker, or acquire some such similar skill. I am not downgrading those skills. In fact, I happen to be a welder and tool and die maker and I also happen to be a process engineer. Yet I do not have the academic qualifications even to start the course in one of these skills under a program for which we pay the bill. The situation is just absurd and as a government we should, in my view, do something to correct it. I do not think we are getting the biggest bang for our dollar in terms of upgrading skills. We should be matching these skills to the opportunities that are available.
Furthermore, Mr. Speaker, in terms of job opportunities and matching of skills a great deal more ought to be done, in spite of the fact that the federal government does not have the constitutional responsibility, to ensure as much as we can by way of advice to ministers of education at the provincial level, to colleges and to universities, that some projection is made of labour force requirements in the future. This would then give us some idea how many lawyers, engineers of various kinds, political scientists or those skilled in academic achievement are required, which information could be made available on a national basis to institutions of learning in the provinces so that those who pass through our universities hopefully can stream themselves, if they choose to do so, into an area of activity which will offer them some hope of finding a job.
If someone wants to go to school for purposes of academic achievement alone, I have no objection. We have lots of room in our society for the thinkers of the world, for the academics who do not want to fall into a specific occupational grouping. However, they would at least be aware that this is the consequence of a course which they chose before they chose it, so that we would not graduate 30,000 political scientists and have

April 18, 1977
The Budget-Mr. Cafik
job opportunities for only eight in the year. That is just nonsense.
Perhaps I may just touch on one or two other matters very briefly. One area I have spoken about before is this. There is a great deal of talk in the mill about family law. One point in this connection I should like to make-I do not know whether I have made the point in the House of Commons but I have spoken about it publicly for about four years-has to do with the concern I have for people with matrimonial difficulties. Take the case of a woman who is deserted by or separated from her husband. There are a number of children the court has awarded alimony for maintenance of the children but the payments do not come through. What recourse does she have? She has to keep going back to the court, which is a costly, time-consuming process. Such a person does not have the means to enforce a garnishee order on wages or anything like that.
Bearing in mind that many of these people receive assistance through social welfare agencies, a process which can go on for years, it seems to me there is room within our system to provide a mechanism whereby awards made for the maintenance of children should be paid by the court, that the court should have the onus of collecting from the person against whom the award is made. The court has the mechanical means whereby the award can be enforced. The court can garnishee wages and can follow a person around to see that the alimony is paid. The present system places too much of a burden upon the individual, and I think in the long run too much of a burden upon society at large in terms of social assistance payments. I think we should do something to help a large number of people who find themselves in a very unfortunate situation in our society today.
Another area I should like to touch on very briefly, Mr. Speaker, has to do with the need to minimize bureaucratic red tape which binds individuals and the business community when dealing with government. The other day in a speech in this chamber I mentioned that I welcomed the steps taken by Statistics Canada to remove a large number of small business people from reporting requirements. I think that was a giant step forward, but there is room for even greater improvement. It seems to me that the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and other federal departments ought to work together in a concerted and co-operative way with provincial governments, perhaps through a federal-provincial conference, to make a very deliberate attempt to minimize this kind of red tape and to provide a genuine-

speechtext: I had to recognize the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra who was standing. The hon. member has the floor.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I was amused to hear the hon. member for Ontario speak. He seems to think that parliament is irrelevant, that parliament can be safely bypassed. I know this is not the first time. In fact, just a month ago the minister responsible for small business made a very important announcement in Vancouver, to which the hon. member for Ontario referred a few minutes ago. Just because more and more ministers are making these announcements outside the House, I do not think this makes it correct. If I may correct the hon. member for Ontario in what he said about the reduction of returns required from small businesses, the Minister of State (Small Businesses) (Mr. Marchand) made it very clear when he was in Vancouver that the reduction of forms to be returned and information sought would save small businesses some $40 million, but that would not be in effect in toto until 1981, some four years away.
The hon. member for Ontario says the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in Winnipeg tonight is doing something for national unity. I was not aware that there were separatist problems in Winnipeg. I think there may be a few in other corners of the country, but not there.
I also think it strange that the hon. member for Ontario thinks that all of the complaints about the budget are coming from this side of the House. I do not know where the hon. member for Ontario spent his Easter recess. Perhaps he was doing something for national unity by staying at home. If he talked to his constituents, he would know that Canadians are worried about this budget and are worried about this country. The hon. member for Ontario does not seem to have been talking to his constituents during the Easter recess.
There are very serious problems in Canada which the budget has done nothing to correct. First, unemployment is expected to continue at record-breaking levels. At present one million Canadians are out of work, and the government has offered no real stimulation of the economy. Second, government deficits are expected to continue to expand out of control. The current deficit is the highest in Canadian history and is greater than the 1964 total of federal government expenditures.
April 18, 1977

Working Canadians will see little for them in this budget with the exception of an increase in the federal tax credit of $50 per child for taxpayers with children, and an increase of $100 in the employment expense deduction limit. Most Canadians will see no effect whatever when they file their 1977 tax returns. It is significant that these changes do not offer any help to pensioners or to the unemployed-only to working Canadians. I am sure most taxpayers were pleased to see the loopholes in the rules covering RRSPs and RHOSPs were closed. This only underlines the government's laxity, since I remember telling the former minister of finance of the RHOSP loopholes after the budget of November, 1974, when it was debated in this House.
If working Canadians see little in the budget, then nonworking Canadians will see utter despair. The Liberal government's attitude used to be epitomized in the expression: "What's a million?" Now it is: "What's a million unemployed?"
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) himself said that the federal government is unable to solve the unemployment problem right away. He said on television earlier this month that he would be as delighted, as any minister of finance would be, to try to get the rate of unemployment down. He went on to say that he did not think we have the tools of a significant magnitude at hand to be able to reduce unemployment drastically. He continued by saying that his budget was not primarily an employment creation measure. What an understatement! At a time when unemployment in Canada has exceeded the one million mark, the government has patted itself on the back for having provided an additional $100 million for the Canada Works program, an amount that will produce an estimated
11,000	jobs. The minister in his budget speech said:
It will have significant impact in reducing the number of unemployed.
His colleague, the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Cullen), also referring to the $100 million said that we will be spending some $1.2 billion on programs for jobs. With one million unemployed, an increase of less than 10 per cent to the government's employment program can hardly be cause to pat oneself on the back.
We on this side of the House understand that the government cannot correct the unemployment problems by direct programs. We have never suggested that the government should be involved in direct job creation. It is true, as the hon. member for Ontario said, that we feel the private sector should and can provide the jobs that are necessary in Canada. However, it can only do that if the government will leave the private sector alone. This $100 million that the government has spoken about will produce 11,000 jobs, but these will not be permanent jobs. They will last only for the duration of the government support. The budget reaffirms that the government has determined that it has neither the intention nor the ability to solve problems of unemployment and that it intends to produce a record deficit of $7,000 million-a deficit of more than $600 for every Canadian taxpayer.
On budget night the Minister of Finance said that without the restoration of confidence we will not generate the jobs we
The Budget-Mr. Clarke
need. He said it in the early part of his speech as though he were heralding budget measures that would attack this basic problem-lack of confidence. No such measures appeared. Of course we in the official opposition have been urging such action for years, and we have not been alone. In February of this year the President of the Institute of Chartered Accountants of British Columbia, W. B. Laurie, urged the federal government to give business and labour specific incentives to deal with Canada's economic woes. He said:
The first gesture to restore confidence should be a general reduction in income taxes, both corporate and personal.
He also said:
A personal tax cut would remove people near the poverty line from the tax rolls and increase consumer spending urgently needed to utilize our excess productive capacity.
That is one of the problems we have in Canada-the lack of demand caused by the stagnant economy that we now have, which produces excessive productive capacity, which costs Canadians dearly.
For years the Progressive Conservative party has been advocating incentives to individuals and business to stimulate the economy and reduce unemployment. It should now be obvious to the government that unemployment and the economy are inextricably bound together. You cannot interfere with business as the government has been doing and expect the private sector to do its job as it should be doing.
Some weeks prior to the budget the leader of my party had outlined a five-part program that would have, first, reaffirmed government's faith in the private sector as the main source of new jobs and new national wealth. Second, it would have assured confidence and certainty in the Canadian economy by eliminating middle of the night rule changes. Third, it would have had different levels of government working together- instead of fighting as at present-to develop a national policy. Fourth, it would have encouraged the placing of savings in equity investment in Canada. Fifth, it would have required the major partners in the economy to resolve the economic problems.
On the eve of the budget my leader speculated that the March 31 budget could be the last chance for Ottawa to bolster the economy. He said that the lack of confidence is critical now, and he called for stimulation of economic growth and significant reductions in personal income taxes. He proposed that the government should reduce the financial demands of productive citizens by curbing federal spending. He also proposed the introduction of a small business investment incentive credit for Canadians who make equity investments in small or medium size businesses. These are the kind of things that will produce jobs in Canada.
It is true that minor measures were taken to help small business by the budget, for example, the extension of investment tax credit, the increase in federal dividend tax credit, and the introduction of inflation adjustment for inventories. But the government has missed the point. Doctor Gail Cook, executive vice-president of the C. D. Howe Research Institute in Montreal, said that the government had not done enough to

April 18, 1977
The Budget-Mr. Clarke
stimulate the private sector. She said that the business community will only invest heavily if it sees an adequate return on its expenditure. The rate of return can only be assured if there is a market for the goods and services. Because of inflation, unemployment and uncertainty, demand for goods and services is shrinking, resulting in reduced sales and climbing inventories.
The further result, and this should be obvious to the government, is increasing unemployment brought about by lay-offs, and the vicious circle begins again.
Joseph Jeffrey, chairman of the London Life Insurance Company, also called for substantial tax cuts for both individuals and corporations-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And he is a Liberal.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
-as a means of reducing Canada's growing unemployment. He said that tax cuts are the ideal method of getting initial money into the hands of consumers and investors. He continued:
New jobs generated would not only tend to offset the tax cuts by generating additional income taxes, but would also reduce government expenditures on unemployment insurance.
The Minister of Finance seems to think that he can save money by keeping people on unemployment insurance rather than giving incentives to the business community which will have the power to take these people off the unemployment insurance rolls. The government seems to be unable to understand that working Canadians are taxpayers while unemployed Canadians are a drain on the taxpayers. I suppose that is not surprising in light of the Prime Minister's comment in the House a month ago when, in answer to a question, he said:
I think that one of the reasons the country is in difficulty is that Canadians are living beyond their means.
In fact it is the government that has been living beyond its means. In the last ten years the federal government has had a budgetary surplus only once, and in every other year it has had to borrow to finance its operations.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Shame!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The figures supplied to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs in March of this year by the Minister of Finance show that Xhe gross national debt on March 31, 1976, stood at over S88,000 million, that is $88 billion in the government's language, but since government ministers do not seem to understand what billions are, I would like to remind them that it is $88,000 million.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Thank you, professor.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
If that sounds like a lot, we can divide it up on a per capita basis and it still comes to over $3,800 of debt per capita in Canada today. As if these heights were not dizzy enough, the government continued to add to this debt at the annual rate of $7 billion, or $7,000 million. Again, for the

benefit of the class opposite, I will translate that. That is $20 million per day. We can break that down a little bit more. It amounts to $820,000 per hour for each 24 hour day.
I think it is interesting to observe that government costs climb fastest in inflationary times. In the later part of 1976, for example, the figures reported that government expenditure was climbing at a rate of 25 per cent per annum compared with an annual rate of 8.8 per cent for inflation. The reason for this was that corporation taxes were falling because of the business climate in Canada, and at the same time personal taxes, because of unemployment and other reasons, were rising less than the government had been expecting. The government continues to ignore what we and others have been telling it, that is, that inflation has been manufactured in Ottawa by excess government spending and excessive growth in our money supply to finance that spending.
Deficits for this year and the past two years have totalled over $17,000 million, an amount equal to two and a half times the aggregate Canadian government deficits in the preceding 30 years. It does not matter how governments try to disguise their taxes, it is the same taxpayers who ultimately must pay the taxes. Governments must tax, borrow, or print more money to cover their spending, but it is taxes that must be collected in the end to pay for current spending, interest on debt, and to repay the debt itself.
During the six years from October, 1970, to October, 1976, federal government current expenditures increased by 151 per cent. To finance this, the money supply was increased in the same period by 100 per cent. While all this was going on the real GNP increased only 31 per cent, and this was an actual decline in the rate of growth over the preceding six year period.
Even though the budget contained measures to increase the investment tax credit in areas of high unemployment, these were certainly overdue. The government claims that 76,000 jobs were created during the last fiscal year, but only 3,000 were created in the five eastern provinces. Why should Quebec have a significantly higher unemployment rate and a significantly higher inflation rate than any of the bordering United States?
I hope that the Prime Minister in his speech tonight in Winnipeg, which is billed as a major address on national unity, will explain what his government intends to do about the regional disparities which have heightened during his term of office, what he plans to do about the unemployed whose benefits have been or will be exhausted, and how he expects to get the real growth in the Atlantic provinces up to national standards. But can we expect such answers from a Prime Minister who in nine years in office has produced the worst economic chaos in history, the worst unemployment in history, and the most divisive attitudes from both ends of the country that Canada has ever seen?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I should like to refer to the remarks of Jacques Parizeau, Quebec's minister of finance. In a recent interview
April 18, 1977

with the Financial Post he described the Trudeau attitude in explaining how Quebec had hoped to cushion the unemploy-, ment problem after Expo '67. This is what Mr. Parizeau said to the Financial Post:
Some of my friends suggest 1 really became a separatist without knowing it after Expo. A ten year old child could well understand that after Expo there would be a terrible unemploymnt crisis in Montreal. So we had to have on the shelves a bank of public works that would have to be plugged in immediately after Expo to take up the slack. This was prepared in 1965, 1966 and 1967. With the federal government we stocked a number of top projects and put them on the shelf for the post-Expo period.
Then our two governments started to fight. That was when Pierre Trudeau was rising in Ottawa and eventually became Prime Minister.
He concluded his remarks as follows:
. .. the whole remarkable program that we had built was completely deserted. Nothing came out of it and we just had to watch unemployment rising in Montreal.
For the leader of our country to treat a single province in a fashion such as that is divisive in itself, and it is no wonder to thinking Canadians that we are having problems with unity today, considering the leadership we have had recently.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He is breaking up the country.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It is well known that we in the official opposition have always opposed long term controls because of the havoc they create. Our 1974 proposal for short term controls, which would have broken the inflation mentality and allowed the government time to adjust its fiscal and monetary policies, was rejected and probably misunderstood by the electorate.
People might have expected some action when 15 months after the 1974 election the government did a complete reversal and imposed controls-for 39 months, it said. However, after 18 months of controls, with confusion and anger rising all over Canada, the government has taken no steps to revise its policies in the direction of responsible financial management. We still had an inflation rate of 9.3 per cent last year, compared with a 5.1 per cent rate in the United States. The government of Canada still continues to grow. Now the Canadian government consumes 43 per cent of our economy, compared with 35 per cent in the United States.
Although when tabling the main estimates for 1977-78 in the House in February, 1977, the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras) said that those estimates should dispel any remaining doubts about the government's determination to restrain the growth of federal outlays, the next month he told a committee of the House that the government will probably not be able to continue present low growth rates in the public service for long.
The former minister of finance in his June, 1975, budget said:
The government proposes to set an example of restraint... by imposing strict control over its activities and programs.
The present Minister of Finance in his May, 1976, budget said:
The Budget-Mr. Clarke
It is a fact of life that the scope for expenditure control increases as one looks further into the future. It proved very difficult to cut back on our expenditures in
1975-	76 once the year was already under way. We were able to get on track for
1976-	77. We will consolidate our gains in 1977-78.
In spite of these declarations and predictions, estimates for 1976-77 were up by 19 per cent, and estimates for 1977-78 show a further increase of 7 per cent, held back somewhat by the transfer of certain burdens to the provinces, but we know that the taxpayer will have to pay it all in the end whether through federal taxes or provincial taxes.
I would like to make a final reference to another area of the budget, where we find that the government is reaching into the graves of Canadian taxpayers. The government was not satisfied with the situation which previously existed, and now it proposes to tax gains on insurance policies which are realized on death. Previously the government was satisfied to tax only the gains which were realized on cashing in a policy, that is, the profit on the investment aspect of the insurance policy.
Furthermore, in addition to reaching into the grave to tax those gains, the government has decided to ignore legitimate loan transactions between policy holders and insurance companies. The minister tried to explain it away by saying there was no obligation to repay a loan. Well, I wonder if the government ever feels any obligation to do anything more than to roll over its own loans. Certainly banks roll over loans. There is plenty of precedent for that. Henceforth, says the budget, interest paid, even on temporary policy loans to enable the taxpayer to launch a business or to tide him over some particular period-he may be buying a house or avoiding a tax discount; it does not matter-will not be deductible under any circumstances. The fact that it was laid out to earn income will be ignored.
All the usual income rules are going to be overlooked. Perhaps to emphasize the inequities of the government's ideas on taxation, existing policy loans will be allowed to continue to bear deductible interest, and that can only be interpreted as a real incentive not to repay existing loans. 1 wonder if the government thought of that when it was entertaining the idea that insurance companies should not have to make loans at the low interest rates they found themselves locked into.
I see it is coming up to six o'clock, Mr. Speaker. In conclusion I say to this House that the record I have sketched today is deplorable and that this budget should be rejected.
