speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I certainly appreciate the opportunity to speak to this budget while being observed from the opposite side of the House by the single hon. member for Edmonton Centre (Mr. Paproski) and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles).

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Except that I am a married member.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
1 realize that is important and 1 have taken note of the fact that we are now ready to begin. With the hon. members on this side and the complement of members on the other side we have a quorum-even though they are only two.
I should like to say that 1 cannot quite understand why there has been such a great gnashing of teeth and screaming and shouting from the opposition parties about this budget. All who looked at the estimates tabled in February could easily have forecast the budget. Although changes could occur in a new budget, the estimates seemed to be geared in a similar direction, in the main estimates, decreases of millions of dollars were forecast. For instance it could be anticipated that the budget decrease for the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources should be about $577.5 million, principally because of the reduction in oil import compensation payments. The Unemployment Insurance Commission decrease was expected to be about $325.5 million. Due to the proposed changes in the established financing formula, the Department of National Health and Welfare's budget was expected to reduce by $172.8 million. A further decrease that seemed to be forecast by the estimates was for the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, $128.5 million, because of reductions in subsidies on the sale of wheat and contracts for grain hopper car fabrication which are now completed. The completion of the 1976 quinquennial census has brought about a reduction of $25.7 million in the budget of Statistics Canada. The Canadian Livestock Feed Board's budget was reduced by $10.9 million due to revisions in the assistance program. This gave a total reduction in the budget of $2,240.9 million.
If we examine the increases in the estimates, they reflect the government's concern for the things that are happening in the country. Although decreases had to be achieved, there also had to be certain increases such as that for the Department of the Secretary of State. Anyone might have forecast that who understood our circumstances at this time. There was a requirement for an additional $567.7 million for post-secondary education and language development.
At least one of the opposition parties has been very vocal as long as 1 have been a member of this House, about the fact that the Department of National Defence should receive attention and that there should be capital expenditures in that department. 1 believe the minister has reflected the desire of the Canadian public to see an Armed Forces presence which
can defend our sovereignty in the north and take care of the establishment of the 200-mile fishing zone, and at the same time be a force we can be proud of and which will service outlying communities. The Department of National Defence received an increase of $423.6 million to cover these expenses.
1 am concerned when 1 hear the cries from the other side of the House that the government does not care for the unemployed. Mr. Speaker, the Department of Manpower and Immigration will receive an increase of $304.3 million to be used to reduce unemployment. There were also cries from the other side about urban affairs. That department will receive an increase of $267.7 million for grants and subsidies to housing and improvement programs in communities. The Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development will receive an increase of $171 million to be passed on to Indian and Eskimo bands and the territorial governments. The Department of Veterans Affairs will receive an increase of $121.3 million to cover higher pensions and allowances. 1 notice the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. MacDonald) applauding, Mr. Speaker. I am sure he would like more but will understand how difficult it is.
The decreases amount to $2,240.9 million and the increases to $1,855.6 million. It is the old story of robbing Peter to pay Paul. When we see how important it is to increase spending in one area we sometimes take the money away from an area we think can spare it, but even then we really know it is not enough for all we want to do. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, the budget might have been forecast.
In the little booklet "Budget in Brief' issued by the Department of Finance, under the heading "Policy Highlights" there appears the following statement:
The federal government will pursue its policy of developing energy supplies. But we must all adopt better conservation practices and face the prospect of higher prices.
The best way for Canadian consumers to protect themselves against higher energy prices is to use less energy.
It was obvious throughout the budget that the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources was attempting to bring that point to our attention.
Some people have complained that nothing was said about controls in the budget or about the fact that this government was once against them. Mr. Speaker, I have no fear of standing before the electorate and saying that I was in a government that brought about a system to try to deal with high inflation and high unemployment. I have no worry about saying that when 1 first came to parliament there was a certain group of people about to go on strike for an increase of 72 per cent; two weeks before we went to a control system. A year later that same group settled for a 6.9 per cent increase instead of 72 per cent because of the initiative of the government. That is on the wage side.
On the price side, it has not been that long since Christmas. As I walked through the supermarkets, I talked to the ordinary people in my constituency. I talked to the union workers at
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. F.thier).]
April 18, 1977

Stelco, Dofasco, Westinghouse, and to electrical engineers. My constituency of Hamilton Mountain is a strong union area.
One wife said, "It is a better Christmas. 1 can do more." That may not sound much to anyone, a better Christmas. Some people asked why we cannot have Christmas all year round. Life does not seem to offer itself in that way. To the ordinary worker, to be able to do something a little special for his family is very important. Many people in my constituency found it possible this past year when it was not possible the previous year.
Price and income controls have helped to bring down the rate of inflation, but their job is not yet done. That is what we are enforcing. When we brought them in most people would not have liked to; we are now saying the same thing and are not afraid to do so.
If controls are suddenly removed, there is a danger that rates of price and cost increases would begin to escalate again. Indeed, 1 attended a meeting with a group of very fine people who were willing to spend an entire Sunday afternoon talking about controls, a group of union workers whom I admire. They spent much time doing research. When one person said "These controls must come off so that we can get a raise which will give us back all that you took away," I could not believe my ears. 1 did not sit and listen to that. 1 could not understand anyone believing that if we removed the system we would go directly back to adjusting all the prices so that people could have all that they would have made, adjusting all the salaries so that people could have what they should have had. If that is what we are going to do, we will go directly back to where we were, where there was such a hardship on the aged and those not unionized, but not for the person with the big salary, the big union, or big business. This Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) is of the conviction that what he is doing is for the most benefit of those most concerned, those who have hardship. Therefore he felt it necessary in this budget to reinforce his opinion of controls.
The government believes it would not be feasible or desirable to begin decontrol before the second anniversary of the anti-inflation program, October 15, 1977. There are many people who are disappointed with that. Regardless of that, 1 have to say that it is a clear cut statement. It is a statement that was asked for, and it is the kind of policy that comes under the budget.
This is not a budget which did not answer questions. It is not a simple stand-pat budget to throw in the faces of people. It is a long-term budget, something that was badly needed. It is something that was placed before us, saying there will not be changes in controls unless the economy itself reflects that it is possible to do so, unless attitudes change and this reflection is there.
A recent business and labour initiative has raised the prospect of sufficient support for voluntary restraint as to warrant consideration of a somewhat earlier decontrol date. That could affect the question of timing. The prospect will be explored in a round of consultations to follow publication of a discussion paper on decontrol and post-control environment.
The Budget-Mr. MacFarlane
In the meantime all parties are advised to proceed with wage and price determination in the expectation that controls will continue in effect for some time. It is not something that this Minister of Finance, this government, or the members of this party say with a lot of ease, but it is something they say without embarrassment, and with strength. They say it to the left, to the right, and to the centre. Controls must not go until there is an indication from the parties concerned that they are willing to co-operate for the benefit of all concerned, and not one at the expense of the other.
What I find surprising is the way in which some people have decried and derided the budget. What worries me is that many of the media and many of the public recognize that these outgrowing policy statements were coming from the budget and they agreed with them, but we continue to get the story that nothing happened.
The government has launched a vast employment strategy keyed to the job creating programs of Canada Works and Young Canada Works. Just today we had a tremendous onslaught, as though every single person who was unemployed is the personal responsibility of someone on this side of the House, and that no one cares.
I hesitate to refer to other countries, but this is an international problem. At the beginning we did not really accept the strategy of freezing prices. We considered inflation at that time to be largely an outside force upon our country. We only went to controls when we saw it become a cost-push situation. We were learning from what was happening outside.
There is no question that the Canadian economy is facing its most serious unemployment problem since the late 1950's. Nobody denies that. However, we are also faced with a whole new set of labour market problems. In the tradition of Liberal governments throughout Canada's history, the present government is responding to these problems with compassion and innovative programs for the individual Canadians who are without jobs.
What are these labour market problems? First, the labour force is growing too fast in terms of the number of job opportunities the economy is generating, even though Canada's employment record has been admirable. In January of this year employment rose sharply, but so did the labour force. In February the labour force increased more than twice as fast as employment rose.
One of the major problems has been the continuing rapid influx of young people and women into the labour market in search of jobs. These two groups of people historically have had the greatest difficulty getting jobs, primarily because many of them are entering the labour market with relatively little experience. As a result, unemployment among youth is now more than two and a half times that of adults.
Youth unemployment in particular is a world-wide phenomenon. The International Labour Organization recently reported that the total of unemployed youth has reached an all-time record of seven million in the world's 24 richest countries. Youth unemployment rates range from an average
80012-211/2

April 18, 1977
The Budget-Mr. MacFarlane
of 28 per cent of total unemployed in Germany to 44 per cent in Great Britain.
Canada has been singled out by other countries as a leader in trying to deal with this tragic problem. United States Senator Elubert Humphrey recently wrote to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Bud Cullen) to say, and I quote:
We are very fortunate in the United States to have a neighbour to the north which not only faces many of the problems of our own economy but which has the leadership and foresight to take innovative approaches to these problems... Our young people will be very fortunate indeed if we in the United States merely follow that lead and establish the same kinds of programs here.
Instead of decrying the programs which exist, we should recognize that these direct employment programs, which are being copied by the United States, France, Australia, and the United Kingdom, among others, rank with the best employment measures in terms of cost per job created and in terms of generating work quickly. In 1977-78 alone almost 90,000 jobs will be created.
Say it is not enough, say we need more, but do not ignore what is happening. Recognize that many people have said, "Do not sponsor it all through government." Why would the Minister of Finance not attempt to influence the economy in a way which would generate the opportunity for private enterprise and private business to do its share in creating new jobs when the Canadian public really want that? We are not in that great socialist society where we are mother and father to everyone. We do have a responsibility and I do think we are fulfilling it in our job creation program. I also believe the Minister of Finance is on the right road in placing responsibility for the creation of jobs on business so that employment might be available for our youth, trained and untrained, in particular, as well as for the women who are looking for employment.
Control over expenditure is certainly evident in the budget. Many of the policies which the people want to see are evidenced there, also. The budget, in itself, has been highly acceptable to business and to the public in general. The only criticism which is anything like sound criticism has come from the labour people who point to the high unemployment figures. But they are not telling the government to stop doing what it is doing. They are saying, "Do more, do more." By the same token, if we were to remove controls and everybody went for the salaries they wanted, more jobs would certainly not be created. There would be less. So I respectfully submit that the budget has been presented in a long term way. And don't forget that our long term now is much shorter than long terms were before; everything has shrunk in time and space and when we talk about a long term now it would appear longer than we would like it, because every day when we have so many unemployed it is a burden upon the Minister of Finance.
Each moment, when we think of the number of people who are unemployed, in Restigouche County, in Hochelaga or Hamilton Mountain or in Vancouver Quadra, is a burden to every one of us. And don't forget that we have members over here who come from areas of terribly high unemployment,

those with the highest percentages, those with 47 per cent. At least in the Maritimes we have almost as many members representing those areas as do the parties opposite; we are as knowledgeable as they are about those areas, and certainly in the great province of Quebec where there is a large amount of unemployment there are ample members on this side of the House who come directly from areas of high unemployment and who are as much concerned as members on the other side are concerned.
Therefore I think we should refrain from simply attacking the budget for its inadequacies, recognizing that certain things might not be possible for a government unless we, in a country which considers itself to be a free enterprise country, can revitalize our economy, revitalize private business, so that it can play its full role in bringing about proper employment.
I should like to conclude by saying one or two words, on a subject which with due respect to the Minister of Finance, is more important to me than the budget. When we talk about the economic situation, when we talk about unemployment, there are many who would like to reverse the cart and say "Because we have poor economics, because we have a problem with finance, because we have unemployment, this problem of alienation has arisen." Let us put that feeling to rest. Let us understand, and let us shout it from the highest hills, that what this country faces today is doubt as to whether it should exist as a country. Let us not allow people in Ontario or in Quebec or in the maritimes or in the plains or the far west or the far north to say, "This is all a dream someone has; there is no problem about national unity; it will go away and disappear." It is serious.
There are some of us who have already started on the road of committing ourselves to ways in which this problem of alienation can be solved for Canadians. If we are Canadians we can centre ourselves upon our unemployment and our poverty, our wealth and our resources together. But if we are not, it will be very difficult to figure out how problems are to be solved. When I think of the people, particularly the Acadi-ans in New Brunswick, or those French-Canadians who live in St. Boniface, I wonder how Mr. Levesque or any of his cabinet ministers can tell them that they don't care or they do care, because that seems to be one technique we hear. They seem to be saying, "We don't care about the French outside; you can handle that; we will handle our situation inside." Or, "We do care about you and it is better for you if we do this."
If they indeed are a separate country, a separate entity with separate sovereignty, how can they tell anybody what to do in Manitoba or in New Brunswick? It is only as Canadians that we don't tell people what they have to do; it is only as Canadians that we can agree how these questions can be solved. It is only when we come to the table as Canadians that our problems can be solved. We cannot come with minds on separation, with ideas as to what the alimony is going to be before we have even accomplished a divorce. We are bound to come to the table as Canadians I have no right to say anything about what is happening in New Brunswick and New Brunswick has no right to ask for any assistance from Ontario, and
April 18, 1977

Ontario has no right to talk about the cost of oil in Alberta, and Alberta has no right to talk about the fact that they did not get enough manufacturing from Ontario out there, or the Crowsnest Pass rates or anything else. We can only talk about these things as Canadians.
I think the national unity situation has a far more important effect on the economy than any simple regulations which are put into force by economic councils or by people who are selling, buying, trading and working. 1 do not think mistakes in financing cause disunity. Disunity is what makes it difficult to share and have a vibrant economy. Thus, in conclusion, 1 make a plea that we should recognize what some of our outstanding Canadians have said.
1 find it interesting from time to time to read what a person like Claude Ryan has said. He hits on the situation easily. He said that one of the great programs was the program which was sponsored by the Christians and Jews across the country under which they exchanged people from Quebec and young people from Ontario. And one day, as we were standing in Central Station and we were making the exchange-people were going back by train to Hamilton or across to Vancouver and the French were going out there and the English were coming in-it was interesting to recognize that those who came from Ontario, who came from Quebec, when they came back they had really gained some English; they had learned some English and they would turn on their TVs and hear English and they would listen to English radio and see English films and hear English music. But the young English who had gone to Quebec would soon quickly forget the language they were supposed to master because the language itself was a little different; it was a little more technical, a little more accurate. The short experience of one month or two weeks, when they went back to an English environment, would all be lost and the real gainers in the language situation were the French Canadians who still had their French because of their background and their culture but who had an English influence to keep their English going.
But, you know, as we stood in Central Station and looked at those young people, we said, "You know, you will never be able again to say to one of those English kids or one of those French kids, 'those other people are foreigners.' " They might not gain equally on the language side but never again would a French Canadian who had spent that month in Hamilton think of English Canadians as foreigners, and never again would the English kid who had lived in Riviere-du-Loup think of French Canadians as foreigners. They would think of them as fellow Canadians. This is important. It is important from my point of view to recognize each other as Canadians.
This is one of the times when 1 would not use French in my speech because 1 would say it is important for English Canadians to stand up without embarrassment and say, "Recognize the French fact." This is not a battle which will be fought in Quebec. There is no room for a battle in Quebec. This is a battle which will be fought in Canada. This is indeed, if you want, a civil war-a war of the mind. We may be able to survive this war of the mind if we act honestly, as English
The Budget-Mr. MacFarlane
Canadians, because I think it is amply proven that even Mr. Levesque is beginning to look at the fact, as he talks about six million, that six million in 21 million is one thing but six million in 246 million is a pretty tough number with which to deal.
We have a chance in Canada to recognize our French brothers as the equals they are. We should listen as Canadians at the table to what they feel is the way that they would feel equal in their country, which is our country as well. This moment is our responsibility, particularly those of us who are Anglophones. Of course it is important that we are able to communicate in the language of the other founding race, as it is important that they communicate with us. But understand the danger, Mr. Speaker, of going down the road to separation. That there is some way whereby some French Canadians might not be allowed to learn English is a horrifying thought. Some English Canadians might then say that they never need to learn French. Indeed, 1 think that we should be learning Spanish, a language which is used by our brothers in South America.
I know that tonight the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) will be speaking about national unity. I regret that I will not be able to hear what he says, but knowing both his spoken and his written word 1 have no doubt that it will be a speech which will be pretty non-political. No one is interested in vote getting, but we are all very much interested in seeing that all Canadians understand at this time that we are being given a great opportunity, an opportunity which comes to nations when they come of age.
When the Japanese came of age, they exported miniature circuits, small radios and television sets all across the world. The Germans gave us the language of science, the technical language of the labs. The Americans and the Russians went to the moon. The Canadian moment is now. What will our export be? Our most important resources, our youth. This is why unemployment is so important to us. Our export will be attitude. Our young people will go across the world and will say, "We worked it out. We are that great"-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have an opportunity to take part in this budget debate on this first day after the Easter recess. Had I spoken prior to Easter I would not have had the opportunity to discuss the pros and cons of the budget with many individuals within as well as outside my constituency, individuals from all political parties and from all walks of life who confirmed their disappointment with and disbelief in this latest budget, particularly as it relates to the unemployed.
During this period of time 1 did have the opportunity to talk to youth from universities and high schools who, contrary to what the hon. member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. MacFarlane) said, were concerned at the fact that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) had told them, "If you want jobs, go elsewhere". They are very concerned about where the government is leading them. They are also very concerned about where the recent budget is going to lead them and the rest of the country.
Another group of people with whom I had the opportunity of speaking, indeed a segment of the economy to which I sent a questionnaire, of which I have the results here, was the business community. I admit that the questionnaire was sent to the small business sector of the industrial community, 73 per cent of which was not content with this latest budget.
However, Mr. Speaker, I would only be echoing the words of those members who took part in this debate prior to Easter if 1 dwelt on the incompetence of the government and its budget to deal with the serious unemployment situation in Canada. The government has in fact not only ignored any prospect of dealing with unemployment but, rather, has budgeted for over one million unemployed in the months and years to come. It was especially my leader, the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Clark), who so eloquently expressed his dismay on one hand, and made very specific recommendations on the other, recommendations dealing not only with the unemployment situation but indeed with the economy as a whole.
In order not to be repetitive, Mr. Speaker, as I said I will not dwell on the subject of unemployment in general terms but rather on a specific area, that area being small and medium size enterprises whose potential employment is not only the biggest in an industrialized nation but certainly the least costly. There is no question in my mind after talking to Canadians in all walks of life that to continue to hand out grants for temporary make-work programs is not the answer. Instead, the emphasis should be put on permanent employment opportunities which can be accomplished by creating strong economic programs within the private sector.
The small and medium owner-managed enterprises, which 1 am talking about, account for over 60 per cent of the labour force in Canada. This is a labour force that is being squeezed under by bureaucratic pressures from all governments across Canada. I am not just referring to the federal government; I am referring to all governments across Canada. This is the labour force that can effectively increase productivity and
April 18, 1977

improve our Gross National Product. This is the labour force whose ranks can invariably include the bulk of the unemployed in Canada, but not if the government continues, as it does, to overlook this vital sector of our economy which forms the backbone of our economic way of life. As a result we are now witnessing the highest rate of bankruptcy in small businesses since Confederation. Should this trend continue, free enterprise as we know it will be damaged beyond repair, only to be replaced by what 1 have often called corporate socialism. The trend will continue unless immediate and positive action is taken by the federal government on this very serious issue.
The government representative of this sector is the Minister of State for Small Businesses (Mr. Marchand). Unfortunately he finds himself with his hands tied behind his back. I have said over and over again in the past how pleased I was that the Prime Minister saw fit to appoint a new Minister of State for Small Businesses. Although I believe the minister is attempting to work in good faith within his portfolio, one must wonder at the credibility of the government when one of its own ministers is not even able to define which segment of the economy falls within his own jurisdiction. 1 am referring to the Minister of State for Small Businesses. When 1 asked the minister on March 24 if he could define small business as it relates to his portfolio, he simply did not have an answer. This is unfortunate, but I do not blame him personally. Obviously he is not allowed to have his own beliefs, concerns or recommendations materialized in cabinet. This is because cabinet obviously has not taken this issue seriously enough to even commit the government, the public and, even more important, the businessmen across the country to initiating today or in the future a small business policy or a small business act.
Small business within this Liberal administration is lost in the void of non-policies. One example of one of the minister's main recommendations to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) for inclusion in this budget was the removal of the capital gains tax on the transfer of a small business from one family member to another. That was a very good recommendation that was made by this party in the past, and by other interested groups such as the Canadian Federation of Independent Business. But there was no mention of this, and many other recommendations made by the minister, made by the opposition parties and special interest groups also were not included in this budget. Unfortunately this only confirms to me my initial reaction that the formation of this small business subministry is simply a temporary move to pacify the disgruntled small businessman rather than for the purpose of creating, outlining and establishing programs and policies, as it should, geared toward the growth and prosperity of the small business sector.
We saw something along those same lines prior to the 1974 election when the ethnic population of this country were disgruntled and the Prime Minister, to appease them, created a ministry or subministry responsible for multiculturalism, only for that ministry to disappear once the Liberals gained a majority in the Flouse.
The Budget-Mr. Jelinek
With unemployment in Canada hovering around the one million mark and no federal intervention to reduce this unemployment in sight, the potential labour growth within this small firms sector can no longer be ignored. In Japan, West Germany and elsewhere, where governments have been concentrating their economic efforts on the well-being of small and medium sized enterprises, populations now find themselves virtually with full employment.
One must reaiize that the most economical form of employment opportunity lies with the entrepreneur who is constantly struggling to avoid the obstacles this government's actions cause to fall in his path. Surely it would not be difficult for the government to reduce the tons of bureaucratic paperwork the small businessman is expected to cope with. 1 know the minister is trying to work hard in this regard, if only the cabinet would untie his hands and the hands of those who are working with him to allow him to make the necessary moves on behalf of the small business community.
Instead of strangling this community, the small business community, with bureaucracy and all sorts of restrictions and controls, it is time that the government initiated forms of incentive instead, be they through the tax system, research and development, or what have you-incentives that would encourage the growth and development of small firms thereby creating built-in employment at the lowest possible cost. This is simply just not happening. In my mind incentive is the key word and one that has disappeared from the political vocabulary in Ottawa today. Instead of incentive programs, we are now in the midst of the greatest give-away era in our history. The higher the number of direct grants or give-aways, the less incentive for realistic productivity. Just as the higher the number of unemployment benefits, the less incentive is there for long range employment.
We can no longer afford to create such temporary make-work programs as to study the usage of washrooms in Canada, which cost the taxpayer $175,000 only to find out that the most dangerous part of the washroom is stepping in and out of a wet bathtub, or to spend $48,000 for a study of fertility of families in Quebec. This has happened. This government gave out grants totalling in the millions of dollars for such purposes as the study of the role of the harmonica in the social culture of each region of Canada. How irresponsible can the government be, particularly when the government itself continues to preach restraint for everybody else except itself?
These are just some of the things which account for the unpredecented spending by this government which now accounts for 43 per cent of the Gross National Product as compared to, for example, 35 per cent of the Gross National Product in the United States. Keep in mind that the bulk of the American Gross National Product is spent on their armed forces, and over-all defence program which, comparatively speaking, does not even affect our Gross National Product in Canada. It makes one wonder, therefore, how the government can be considering proposals for the indexing of pensions to the cost of living for federal civil servants, members of parliament, and senators. There is no way, in my opinion, that we can

April 18, 1977
The Budget-Mr. Jelinek
afford to do this today, let alone force it upon future governments and generations. To go ahead with such a proposal on indexed pensions is irresponsible and would be the first step toward the unpredecented and ultimate bankruptcy of the government, and therefore possibly of the country as a whole. Even this government can only continue to print money for so long.
It has been said over and over again, and it must continue to be said, that the government must curb its expenditures to at least the levels of controls which it imposes on both the public and private sectors. Our party and our finance critic in the last Speech from the Throne, or in the last budget debate before this, brought out in detailed form how this can be achieved by reducing government spending by around $1 billion. Instead of printing more money, which is the major cause of inflation, the growth in the money supply must be reduced. This must be done fast.
Specific economic problems and remedies undoubtedly vary from country to country and region to region. However, general economic problems are indeed universal. Having travelled throughout my life throughout many parts of the world and, more specifically, having recently completed a national tour across Canada, this time for the purpose of discussing mutual problems and potential solutions with small businessmen, I was somewhat pleasantly surprised to find how common these problems and potential solutions were in this regionalized country of ours. Business in general, but small businesses in particular, unite this country as no other segment of our economy does. The problems, concerns, the mutual understanding reached in Victoria, are viewed in exactly the same way in Toronto, Quebec City or Halifax. Yet the threat of separation and the ultimate breakup of Canada are seemingly hovering over all Canadians today.
It has now become evident from numerous polls that the majority of Canadians do not want Quebec, or for that matter any part of Canada, to leave Confederation. The results of my own constituency questionnaire on this matter showed that
90.1	per cent of my constituents oppose separation in any form. The British North America Act which provided Canada's Constitution also provides that in a sufficiently great emergency the federal parliament has the power to deal adequately with that emergency for the safety of Canada as a whole, even though it might thereby interfere with property and civil rights in the provinces. I bring this forward because surely the threat of separation can be considered to be an emergency and therefore the federal parliament could state that under the BNA Act no province can withdraw unilaterally from Canada. There is no doubt that such legislation would be acceptable to almost all Canadians, including a majority of citizens in the province of Quebec, and it should be enacted before a referendum on separation is held by Mr. Levesque.
The fact that the possibility of a breakup of Canada as we know it does exist naturally makes the threat of separation a priority issue, thereby overshadowing the serious implications

of an economic slowdown and a lack of action by governments to deal with this slowdown. Unless and until that threat is overcome, Canadians will continue to suffer the consequences of an ill-managed economic policy. That is why I urge honourable members to consider the possibility of referring to those provisions in dealing with the emergency we are now facing and calling on the government to put forward a piece of legislation officially prohibiting the separation of any part of Canada, thereby closing any further dialogue on this matter.
Canadians do not want any part of Canada to separate, and we are wasting our time which could be spent more profitably on debating important issues such as the economy. It is true that a dialogue on this issue is taking place, as well as on other issues, but perhaps there is not enough of it. Government members are concerned and opposition members advocate their recommendations, cabinet ministers become involved and the public voices its opinion through various polls, talk shows, letters, phone calls, and so on. Of course this is a healthy democratic process, but it stops at the doors to the Prime Minister's office. Beyond those doors the Prime Minister does not care, and I do not think he even knows what is happening, and certainly he does not value the opinions of members of parliament from either side of the House or the feelings of Canadians, nor even at times the recommendations of his own cabinet ministers. The latter is evidenced by the record number of resignations and defections from his cabinet during his reign as king Pierre.

But he does not, as has been evidenced over and over again during his time as Prime Minister.
Even though the Prime Minister may at times appear brave and firm, one must begin to wonder about his growing lack of credibility which has become apparent. Less than one year after he said "separation is dead", the Prime Minister is trying to polarize the issue. Less than one year after he said "inflation and unemployment are beaten"-

The Prime Minister's capacity to unite this country and bring a semblance of order to our economy has been clearly demonstrated over the past nine years. To those of his supporters who do not believe this, let me say it again. In the last nine years the capability of the Prime Minister to bring this country to its present situation has been
April 18, 1977

demonstrated, whether it be in the sphere of economics or of unity. Economically speaking we are in the worst mess we have ever been, and so far as unity is concerned, we all know where we stand.

It is unfortunate that the Prime Minister very seldom addresses the House of Commons when speaking on important issues such as unemployment. I believe he learned his lesson when he ran head on into the Leader of the Opposition on the last budget. The Prime Minister himself admitted-and it is on the record-that that day he was no match for the Leader of the Opposition. Perhaps that is why the Prime Minister is afraid to come to the House of Commons to face this side. He has to go to Washington to make policy speeches and he has to go to Winnipeg to make policy speeches, but he does not come to parliament where he is supposed to make policy speeches.
One of the biggest mouths on the other side is that of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) who is making interjections during my speech. I remember very distinctly, when fitness and amateur sport were still in the minister's lap, that as the official opposition critic on sport and fitness I recommended that there should be a sub-ministry for fitness and amateur sport. The Minister of National Health and Welfare then spoke to a sports association at the Chateau Laurier, laughed at the recommendations of the hon. member for High Park-Humber Valley and spoke about how impossible it was to have a sub-ministry for fitness and amateur sport. He thought it was a ridiculous recommendation, but then a few months later, as is characteristic of this government, there was a big flip-flop, and we now have a Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport) (Mrs. Campagnolo).

It is time the Prime Minister's capacity to unite this country and bring a semblance of order to our economy was used.
In closing, we must not allow anyone to change the basis of what Canada and Canadians stand for, even though the Prime Minister has said that the free market system will not work. Hon. members opposite and hon. members on all sides are concerned because unity is difficult to attain. As Canadians, new and old, we must unite this country through co-operation, understanding, and reasonable compromise, and not permit any minority to suffer the injustices of restraint of freedom, whether that freedom be freedom of religion, education, business or language.
As an elected representative, but far more important, as a Canadian, I will continue to stand strongly behind these principles, which are the very foundation of this great nation.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a duty for hon. members to take part in the important budget debate. Evidently, and I would like to make my brief comments in that context, each member on this side of the House could make partisan comments, as we have heard some, holding the government responsible for every evil and adding that if they were in power they could do better. We might also hear members opposite say that everything is all right and that if the opposition were in power, conditions would not improve. At any rate, Mr. Speaker, I do not think that Canadians would be further ahead if the budget debate failed to reach a higher level.
In my opinion, the budget speech must be considered as an approach by this government to the economic problems confronting our country and our fellow citizens. I think it is the duty of members of the opposition to judge the contents of the budget speech not as a whole but in a detailed and thorough fashion. Mr. Speaker, I would like to refer to a special phrase which came to my mind when I received, as did all members, a letter dated April 15 from the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) advising me as follows:
Dear Member of Parliament:
As you are aware, in his recent budget speech the Minister of Finance announced the allocation of an additional $100 million for our employment strategy. On April 4, 1977, following that announcement, I therefore informed the House that $50 million would go to the current phase of Canada Works and $20 million to Young Canada Works.
In his letter, the minister informs each of the 264 members of Parliament of the budgets based on the real unemployment rates in our respective constituencies, of what would be spent in them. From the outset all members received that kind of letter from the minister, not long after the announcement of the new program, which was supposed to replace the old Local Initiatives Program, also a temporary job-creation program, based on people's initiatives and ideas.
4742

April 18, 1977
The Budget-Mr. Fortin
Well then, to speak of something more concrete, the riding of Lotbiniere was granted the sum of $275,000 under the Canada Works program. In that letter, the Minister told me, like all other members, that if I wanted I could set up an advisory committee composed of representative constituents. Like many other members, regardless of political parties, I therefore set up such a committee, not to accept or reject projects, but to classify them in priority order. The budget was then $275,000, based on the real unemployment rate which was arrived at by using the statistics of manpower centres.
Then the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) rose and, faced with an incredible level of unemployment which is affecting young people most, he announced in his budget speech higher expenditures, as 1 indicated in my previous quotation, which will increase the amount of $275,000 granted to the Lotbiniere constituency by $238,000 to a total of $513,000. The same applies to the Young Canada Works program, for a little while after the budget speech, the minister increased by $131,000 to $301,000 the amount of $170,000 which had been originally earmarked for the Lotbiniere constituency.
Mr. Speaker, I make the following remarks free of partisanship, for I have this matter very much at heart. Of course, as all other hon. members, I am glad the government agreed to invest large amounts of money in my riding to create employment. So much so because the people in my riding are really involved in worthwhile projects. Mr. Speaker, the remarks I should like to make are at this level. From the start, the minister wrote to me. He asked me to volunteer to sit on the advisory committee which would study each project and rank them according to their priority in relation with the real needs of the constituency. Those needs were established by officials who do their work well and by citizens approved by the minister. Those people meet seriously, make a serious study, and finally suggest a series of projects to the minister in a process of elimination.
As everyone knows, the elimination is done within the limits of the budget. Everyone is happy except those whose project was refused because of insufficient funds, who go back to the manpower centre, change location, move, find employment elsewhere, and completely abandon their project and hope that it will be accepted during the second phase. Now, Mr. Speaker, during the budget debate, to appease somewhat the virulent and justified criticism of the government inaction-I mean its long term inaction to eradicate unemployment in Canada-the minister announces that the initial budget will be nearly doubled, so that now, with no thought given to the initial work of consultation and the meetings held by these people, certain projects which were given more or less priority will now be Financed. The same thing will probably happen with the Young Canada Works program.
Mr. Speaker, the same thing happened with the Local Initiatives Program in Lotbiniere, and probably in many other constituencies. First the government promises us a certain

budget and takes the trouble to state that there will be no budgetary increase. People then go back home grumbling and try to meet requirements. A non-political choice of the projects is made since the advisory committee removes all political aspects from its choice, but after this has been done, a month, a month and a half, two months later, the same minister or another one, the Minister of Finance this time, stands up and announces that the budget has been nearly doubled.
In all honesty, Mr. Speaker, I humbly admit that I am very happy to see even more money come to us, like all my colleagues, but this shows that this government, like the previous ones, has no long term industrial strategy not only to create jobs, but to maintain them. This is why, Mr. Speaker, the temporary job creation programs which come up one after the other were invented a few years ago. There was Opportunities for Youth, which no longer exists. Then, there was the Company of Young Canadians, which no longer exists. Then, there was the Local Initiatives Program, which is now gone. We now have Canada Works, and one day, probably very soon, this will disappear to be replaced by another program. We now have Young Canada Works.
That is a bad approach. False hopes are generated among people. Those people sit down around a table and detect problems, hon. members and concerned citizens set priorities on projects and then, all of a sudden, everything is turned upside down, we start all over again and we finance almost anything. I think that every member, when he really thinks about it, will have to admit that this conclusion is right. That reflects a fact.
Of course, Mr. Speaker, an hon. member could ask the minister to double his budget. Surely if the Minister of Finance would agree to do that for the constituency of Lotbiniere, I would be very happy with that but, to be honest, I do not think we have enough good projects which could be properly financed or deserve to be financed.
Mr. Speaker, in my constituency, we are trying at the same time to deal with the unemployment problem through federal government programs which, I repeat, are temporary and shortsighted and are doubled or scratched overnight. Those are decisions I would not dare qualify as political, but they are indeed very questionable. Simultaneously we see the systematic disappearance of jobs in the textile and furniture industries. This last month and a half, I visited about 40 plants in Quebec, Alberta and Saskatchewan. I met with the workers. I also met with quite a lot of unemployed. This Canadian trip showed me that Canadians are ready to build this country. What they lack first is work incentive, second, job protection and third, economic leadership from the government.
Coming back to the first point, Mr. Speaker, I would say that import controls are essential. Hundreds and thousands of jobs are lost in Quebec and in other provinces simply because while the government establish temporary job creating programs, often of a social nature, they open our doors to textiles imported from Japan, Taiwan, Korea or elsewhere, they permit competition, particularly from the United States in the furniture business, and this competes with our own jobs in
April 18, 1977

Canada; this is how our jobs and industries which formed the economic backbone of our regional structures disappear gradually.
In the meantime, the government introduced this kind of "shortsighted" program, Mr. Speaker, to compensate a little and to appease the passions and the pressing demands on the part of the citizens. So when programs such as LIP or Canada Works or Opportunities for Youth or Young Canada Works are ended, all we hear is this: this project should continue, Mr. Fortin; it was so fantastic, and once again, hon. members will agree with me. It is obvious that it was "so fantastic , but the only answer we can give is that we do not know, that it is a temporary program and we wait for the minister's answer. Maybe yes, maybe no. We do not know.
All members in their constituency offices had to answer the many requests by citizens who had a project and wished to go on with it, instead of being faced with unemployment, who wanted to continue their project because they identified a need, because they would like to improve or amplify, extend or diversify their project. We do not know, we are waiting.
Then the minister gets involved. We do not know for what reason, we do not know within which industrial strategy, job creation or existing job maintenance programs, but here comes the minister announcing in a letter that the constituency of Lotbiniere will get a budget of $275,000. Then everything is under way. But two months later we receive another letter from the minister after projects have been accepted, given priority, put in order, sent to the minister, once they are under way, the sponsors have gone elsewhere, the minister writes to us saying:
"Well now, boys, go on working, be earnest, be honest, we have new money in store for you. Go ahead! This is totally ridiculous, Mr. Speaker. We shall never build a country with such a near-sighted approach. This is what I would like hon. members to realize. Whether our constituencies elected a Progressive Conservative, Liberal, Social Credit or New Democrat member, we all experience the same problems each day. In my area as elsewhere, there were some projects probably fantastic in nature. Some were less so, but many were fantastic. However, nearing termination people came to me and asked: "Mr. Fortin, what are our chances of continuing?" What answer can we give? We are members here, we ask the government or we write the minister about their future plans. They do not know, we have no inkling, not a word. And then, suddenly, we get a letter and here we go again!
This is playing with people's good faith. The government is now forced to establish that kind of temporary program, that kind of band-aid, not because it is a Liberal government, but because it has no industrial strategy approach of any kind.
Second, the government is not interested in fighting unemployment. It has other financial interests to pursue. The proof is, and I would like to stress this, they allow an uninterrupted flow of textile imports, polyester fibers for instance and others from abroad, to compete here with our own Quebec and
The Budget-Mr. Fortin
Canadian products. Of course businessmen and consumers will buy what looks to be the best quality at the cheapest price, so our Canadian products remain unsold, employment is reduced, unemployment is on the rise. Simultaneously, the government says: "Use restraint, we must fight inflation, we must control wages and salaries-but not prices". Canadian products are getting more expensive all the time, they cannot compete with imports from countries that sometimes or quite often exploit cheap labour. And that is how, Mr. Speaker, when fighting inflation at consumers' and workers' expenses, we allow imports to enter this country to compete against our own workers with our own products and thus increase our unemployment rate. Those are the main sources of dissension in this country.
Mr. Speaker, we see one Canadian or one Quebecer unemployed for five or six months. How could this man have any ambition to build his country? He feels rejected from the community and he feels he must depend on it to survive, and he is finally the victim of the bureaucracy of the Unemployment Insurance Commission. And the government does not know what to do with him because there are too many like him. We have now the highest rate of unemployment in 37 years. We have one million jobless workers in Canada. In 1977, with a majority government, what is the problem, Mr. Speaker? The individual who has been unemployed for five or six months lives through a deep human tragedy. He feels more and more dependent on society and workers feel in turn that they are supporting him doing nothing.
And that is why the unemployed and the workers are divided, why they tear one another to pieces and fight one another. Why? Because there are no equal opportunities in this country, because job opportunities are more than scarce, they are practically non-existent. Why? Because this government is not on the side of the poor and the worker. Why does this government not have an import control policy? Will this industry have to disappear before the government wakes up?
We used to have a very prosperous footwear industry in Quebec, but it has now disappeared and we are wearing imported shoes. That is shocking. It is not a political fact, it is an economic reality. We are paying more and more taxes, and the last budget brought down by the Minister of Finance is in no way different from previous budgets. It is exactly the same dish served differently. There is nothing new there. Taxes are still there. Most are higher. Austerity is the word. Tighten your belts. No long-term job creation program. No guarantee that existing jobs will be protected. But, good heavens, Mr. Speaker, where is this going to lead us? I say that the time has come to stop playing politics with these issues.
For a long time, the Social Credit has been advocating as a long-term measure a more flexible taxation level and the use of the Bank of Canada to finance the public sector, not the private but the public sector, so as to give a new impetus to our productivity and provide some relief to the taxpayers. I know full well that makes a lot of people laugh. Mr. Speaker, in the present traditional context, neither the Tories nor the Grits have anything other to suggest, in order to increase our
80012-2 2Vi

April 18, 1977
The Budget-Mr. Fortin
productivity and better distribute Canadian wealth, than inviting foreigners to come and invest in Canada. It would seem that, were it not for foreign investments in our country, it could not operate.
When we, Social Crediters, suggest using the Bank of Canada to develop and finance the public sector, the traditional politicians, Tories and Grits alike, laugh at us, and find the suggestion amusing. They would rather borrow from abroad and bring in money to Canada to build a school, highway, or bridge. With that system, the government is of course obliged to levy taxes representing two, three or even four times the real cost of the construction, in order to pay back the capital and interest. Some hon. members do not believe that; yet those very same members are very much concerned about the future of our country.
Well, Mr. Speaker, some hon. members may not be aware of it but there is in Quebec a corporation known as the Quebec Housing Corporation. That corporation is responsible for the construction of low-cost housing for the aged. It gets its funds from the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation in Ottawa.
To build 35 units, and my colleague from Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert) as well as others have already spoken about that in the House, the CMHC loaned Quebec $563,000 to be paid back by the Quebecers over a 50-year period. The rate of interest charged by the federal government to the province of Quebec is 10 per cent compounded, so that, after 50 years, the Quebecers will have paid Ottawa five times the initial amount of $563,000. And after a thing like that, one would call it federalism and talk about a constitutional problem in Canada? No! The problem is one of economics based on the mode of financing both the public sector and the provinces.
If the separatist movement in Quebec is gaining ground, Mr. Speaker, it is because many Quebecers are more and more aware of such exploitation of a government by another. I say this not because I am a separatist. I love my country, I believe in Canada. But I do not understand that for most federal members, it is more important to support their own political party and to follow the same beaten track that has led us to our present failure, instead of trying to join forces in order to build a new Canada with modern tools and to finance our development.
I fail to understand how, because of their petty partisanry, our federal members in general are making it impossible not only to preserve our national unity but to maintain a country strong and able to develop and build itself. Since when do we depend on foreign capital to build our country? Since when do Canadians not have enough confidence in their own country to the extent of having to depend entirely on foreign finance for the development of their own public projects like the Olympic Games, James Bay, Hydro Quebec, Hydro Ontario, and so on? Since when?
What is the difference between $100 million from Wall Street, New York, and $100 million from the Bank of Canada? In both cases, those $100 million increase the Canadian purchasing power and we shall have to tax our
(Mr. Fortin ]
citizens in order to repay the borrowed capital. And according to the proposal of the Social Credit, we would repay the capital plus 1, 2 or 3 per cent for administration costs. Under the present system, we have to tax our citizens four and five times for the capital borrowed from foreign sources in order to develop our own country.
Mr. Speaker, I find it terribly dismaying to see the Quebec premier having to go to explain his policy on Wall Street, New York, as I find terribly dismaying to see the Prime Minister of my country going to Washington to explain Canadian internal problems, just as I find it extremely depressing to see the Manitoba or Saskatchewan premiers borrowing money from the Americans to finance public development projects in their own province. We have something in common in Canada and that is our collective hat-in-hand approach with regards to public financing.
Mr. Speaker, this country is very diversified, very wast. British Columbia gave itself a Social Credit government. Alberta elected a Conservative government. Saskatchewan and Manitoba opted for the New Democrats. The Ontario government is straddling the fence, neither Conservative, NDP or totally Liberal. Quebec chose the Parti Quebecois government and I could go on, to show how Quebecers, and Albertans or Manitobans do not agree in a Canadian concensus with regards to self-financing, self-government. Whether it be the Prime Minister or the Leader of the Opposition, through one party or the other, all hon. members here assembled would like to keep this country united.
Mr. Speaker, that will not be possible as long as we do not make it a political issue. We will have to agree with each other now that we have learned to live together for 110 years; we will have to review our institutions, turn the page and look to the future. Are we or are we not proud to be Canadians? Do we believe in this country or not? Such is our choice and I truly believe, Mr. Speaker, that if the referendum were to be called tomorrow morning in Quebec, the federalists would have practically no chance of coming through. And that for a very simple reason: the federalists themselves see the success or failure of this referendum as a personal political victory and not as the need to learn to live together in this great and vast nation.
Mr. Speaker, that is fundamental. I talked to some people in Manitoba, Alberta and Saskatchewan. We must go over there.
I talked to some people in Thetford Mines, in Quebec City, in Montreal, in SherDrooke, and all Canadians, English-speaking and French-speaking alike, have lost confidence. They feel that they can no longer get the attention of their Parliament and their government and that they are completely cut off from their elected leaders. Generally speaking, Canadians feel that they no longer participate in the economic development of this country.
I ask the government to indicate to me a program effectively promoting work, encouraging development of small business in this country. Quite the contrary, we now have one million unemployed and as many people on public welfare. When we complete our income tax returns, Mr. Speaker, we realize that
April 18, 1977

it was wasteful to work for this country because we end up being penalized. Let us consider the cost of housing in this country. It is an outright rip-off. The same for interest rates. A young married couple will have to pay back three, four and five times the cost of their house, even that is only a house, but all through their life they will be ripped off by the financial system, only to have a place to raise their family. Let us have a look at the government approach in the federal budget as well as in the Quebec budget which levies taxes on children's clothing-

speechtext: 1 regret to interrupt the hon. member but the time allotted to him has expired. He may continue with the unanimous consent of the House. Is that agreed?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
