subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I shall be very brief, Mr. Speaker, and I thank my colleagues for their kindness.
As I was saying, let us look at the content of federal and provincial estimates, it is not a matter of partisanship but of personal conviction. They are destroying the family concept in this country simply because they fail to encourage the individual in his work to support his family, and the wife is even forced to work. Why? Because wages are inadequate, employment is rare, the cost of living is high and domestic needs are very costly.
Lo and behold, they are going to tax children's wear in Quebec. Here in Ottawa, the exemptions announced in this budget regarding children, the first, the second, the third and the fourth, are totally unacceptable. It is a national disgrace, Mr. Speaker. And this is not because they are put forward by the present government, the whole approach is wrong, and is it any wonder that this country is no longer united? The basis of this country is family unity and since it was destroyed, Mr. Speaker, let us not be surprised by what we are going to reap.
The right hon. Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Trudeau), instead of going on a trip to Winnipeg, should rather try to initiate frank, honest and open discussions with the Quebec government as well as the government of other provinces, rather than seeking confrontation as it has done since November 15.
Mr. Speaker, this is essential. What is to be earned through this kind of day to day confrontation? It is impossible to watch the newsreport on television in the evening without seeing a Quebec minister take a stand against a federal minister, and vice versa. It is distressing. And they say they would like to negotiate! But, Mr. Speaker, we shall never build a country on this kind of narrow-minded discussions. Why do we not simply think Canadian? Why do we not try to be united and to learn how to live together? Why do we not get over the past and keep the good things it brought us, and build a future in giving ourselves modern institutions? It is a disgrace to keep the other
The Budget-Mr. Hopkins
place in its present state, Mr. Speaker. When one thinks, for instance, that the former member for Langelier (Mr. Mar-chand) has resigned from his position, went to run for the Quebec election and was rejected by the people there finally to be appointed in the other place! What credibility is this institution supposed to have for the Canadian people?
Mr. Speaker, I sincerely hope that my colleagues will think about it and consider the future of this country not in a partisan way but as Canadians, proud of being so.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I had started out my first sentence by saying, "I am going to start off my remarks tonight with what might be considered to be a rather unusual approach". Indeed, it is more unusual than I had anticipated, because if I heard the hon. member for High Park-Humber Valley (Mr. Jelinek) correctly he said something to the effect that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) was afraid to speak in this House because he would run headlong into the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark). Well, Mr. Speaker, the Leader of the Opposition does not spend enough time in this House to run into anyone or anything.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Ha, ha, ha!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I should like to go back a few years, because history is very important to a nation. 1 recall that when I was attending university I had what I considered to be the privilege of studying under a very interesting professor whose predictions of that day and indeed whose predictions during previous days, have unfolded into what one might describe now as historical truths. He always referred to any young students who had any radical ideas about politics, history or sociology as his group of angry young men. We did have, and we still do have, a few of them in this Chamber and they have added considerably to the interest in our debates and to the usefulness of the House. He always referred to any of the ladies in the class as some of the people of the future. It was never really his tradition to mention them very often. Women's lib was not at its highest point at that stage and I doubt if that particular thought had ever entered his mind at that time.
While he was talking about some of the young people of that day as being angry young men, I cannot help but wonder if he fully realized that many of us in his class certainly looked upon him, in a kindly sense, as somewhat of the angry old man of that day who was driving some of us forward. I am speaking here of Dr. Arthur R. M. Lower, Ph.D., F.R.S.C., professor of history at Queen's University, Kingston, sometime professor of history and political science at United College, Winnipeg. This man had an insight into Canadian history to such a degree that he literally predicted what this country is going through today. I am glad to see the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) applauding Dr. Lower because I look upon his as one of the outstanding intellects of that day.

April 18, 1977
The Budget-Mr. Hopkins

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You were lucky to be his student.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I certainly was. He once said about Canada that if it were internationally unreliable it might attract as much attention as Ireland or Italy; but since it can invariably be counted on in advance by the powers to whom its conduct matters, it ranks as safe and sane, a successful mediocrity of a country, like Switzerland or Sweden. He also stated that writing Canadian history remains an act of faith, the substance of things hoped for. His book entitled "Colony To Nation" was finished in the last year of the second world war and the fourth printing of that book took place in September of 1951.
An interesting part of it all is that many of the things he had to say in those days have since played a major role in our contemporary times, and yet I would have to judge that not very many of his students in the mid-fifties would have really believed or understood the full impact of what he was saying. For example, when we take into consideration his statement that "the writing of Canadian history remains an act of faith, the substance of things hoped for", this indeed leads us into the field of practical politics itself.
He went on to say:
Yet it is no lack of great themes that has prevented the history of Canada in this sense from being written, for the four centuries of the country's existence abound in themes which appeal not only to the analyzing intellect but to the imagination. If people find Canadian history dull, it must either be because they are dull themselves or because the Canadian historic scene has not yet been painted in its own bold colours. How could a history full of grandiose projects, startling contrasts, stark antitheses, be dull? How could significance be lacking in the story of a country whose very existence consists in a never-ending battle to accomplish the impossible?
Here we find his penetrating mind provoking our thoughts and prodding us into a state of imagination and reality at the same time. During every lecture that I recall that he ever delivered, he put tremendous emphasis on the two major racial groups of Canada and the problems that existed between the two, and felt that some day those problems would come out in the open and cause this country to face the stark reality of two different cultures, in the same way that you have two sleeping giants who suddenly come to life and realize that each other is present.
It did not seem difficult to him that on future occasions Canada would again be facing difficulties of national unity, because he himself had written many realistic examples of the problems that existed between the two major groups during the course of his own lifetime. At the same time he was a man who did not treat history as a number of facts and figures and dates and romantic fictional stories; rather he treated history as a real analysis of men's approach to each other and, on the basis of an immense background of study of such analyses, then proceeded to make projections and predictions for the future.
In other words, he was a man with a great perspective. For example, this angry old man-and I use this term in a very kind and respectful sense-stated:

Unique solutions, founded on unwilling tolerance, have been reached by Canadians for these overwhelming problems of theirs. "Responsible government", the compromise between imperialism and colonialism, or between dependence and independence, was worked out on Canadian soil and by Canadians: The Federal Union of 1867, which through mutual agreement to forgive and forget opened a way to solving the problem of the conquest of 1763, was in itself one of the greatest acts of statesmanship in the 19th century; the bold defiance of geography contained in the national planning which was an essential aspect of Confederation resulted in the integration of half a continent.
In these lines, and later on in many of his writings and indeed in many of his lectures, he brought to bear on the minds of his students the very complex problems that faced Canada because of regional differences and major cultural differences that must be respected and recognized in a sort of gentleman's agreement if Canada were to survive as an integrated and united nation.
About his own book he said:
This book has been built about some of these great themes. The author hopes that a careful reading of his pages will help Canadians to some of that self-knowledge so necessary if they are to take their rightful place in the world, and still more, if they are to be a happy people, at peace with themselves. If he has not succeeded in this task, then someone else must take it up, for it is imperative. It may be performed by the statesman, by the novelist or the poet, or it may be performed by the historian. Certainly on no one is the duty of revealing to the people, reasons for the faith that is in them, more directly laid than on the historian, for by its history a people lives.
I would like to repeat that "by its history a people lives." Today we find ourselves facing grave problems of national unity in Canada. It is a time when we must not be looking at our present day problems in a contemporary sense alone. We must be looking at them and at our regional problems with a perspective of past history in mind, with a sincere sense of duty and indeed desire, and possibly above all with courage and imagination based on past history, and our present and future outlook, if we are going to tackle the real, basic problems of national unity with a degree of in depth reality.
At this point I would like to pay an outstanding tribute to my federal colleagues from the province of Quebec and from other regions of Canada, who are putting forth a sincere and constructive effort to hold this nation together.
What we need today and what we are going to continue to need in the days ahead are people on both sides of this parliament who possess the faith, the determination, and the courage of the Fathers of Confederation of this nation, those Fathers of Confederation whom we can gaze upon in those large portraits on the walls of the Railway Committee Room, which we view from time to time, and in no one in this House are that faith and determination for a united and continuing Canada better exemplified than in our present Prime Minister of Canada.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
At mid-century, Professor Arthur R. M. Lower went on to say something that today we can look upon with a great sense of irony:
For Canada itself, the glass at the half-century mark stands fair. Relationships between the two races are more cordial than normal; one sometimes wonders,
April 18, 1977

indeed, how long such unnatural conditions can continue. The English-speaking world is still in harmony and, consequently, English-Canadian souls are also resting in peace. A new province has been added: its reception into the family was cordial and the average English-Canadian even allowed himself a barely observable flicker of national emotion over the event.
In this particular statement, he is obviously telling us that up until the middle of the twentieth century Canadians had never really become overly enthused about their own nation, or indeed about their strong desire to build a good future for this country. 1 am sure that he felt in his day that a great sense of national pride was somewhat lacking.
I, and 1 am sure many or most members in this House, would readily agree that such is not the case in our contemporary times. I can well recall that when I was in Grade 11 in a high school in Ontario, I got involved in a rather unseemly argument with my history teacher because I was very strongly in support of a truly national Canadian flag, and as a result, 1 was treated like somewhat of a rebel or even an anarchist. One of my long-standing regrets has been that I was not a member of this parliament when Canada's national flag was finally adopted after many, many weeks of bitter debate and anxious moments.
Today is not a time for political opportunism, nor is it a time for national weakness. It is a time for Canadians with moral fibre; it is a time for Canadians with constructive and federalist ideals; it is a time for all Canadians to converse together; it is a time for all Canadians to think together; it is a time for all Canadians to understand together; and it is a time for all Canadians, indeed, to stand together. As an author once said:
Even the woodpecker owes his success to the fact that he uses his head and keeps pecking away until he finishes the job he starts.
In our generation and in the next we must continue to finish the job that was started by the Fathers of Confederation and successive statesmen of Canada. Like those Fathers of Confederation we must not play the role of the pessimist who sees a difficulty in every opportunity. Instead, we must play the role of the optimist who sees an opportunity in every difficulty, and in particular in those we face today in the field of national unity.
At this point in time one must consider that Dr. Lower when writing his book "Colony to Nation" was not in a position to assess the growing and long term development and public impact of mass electronic media in the field of television in particular, and in the continued extension of radio services in general.
As recent events have shown, our dedicated federalists in this country have proven themselves courageous enough to stand up and be counted and accused the television network of promoting many of the problems of national unity that we face today. Because the CBC network was fostered, among other things, to promote national unity, then there should be no question but that that is the purpose for which it must stand. While the CBC French television network has come in for special criticism with regard to charges of bias on its part, there are other areas of CBC broadcasting and telecasting that should come under scrutiny as well. Before going into one or two of these I would like to emphasize very strongly that I am
Adjournment Debate
not generalizing with regard to my comments about the CBC because there are really many very informative and worthwhile programs. It would be wrong to condemn the good along with the bad, and I would not want those who are trying to be fair and informative to be thrown into the same bag with all the others who are accused of being biased and unfair.
There is no question about the existence of a very strong bias in the CBC with respect to nuclear energy. I would like to exemplify that statement by quoting a letter that I received from one of my constituents. He wrote a letter to the CBC to register a complaint against the program "Concern" that was broadcast on October 20, 1976. I should also add that this is only one of several letters that I received on the same topic and program. It is headlined: Deep River, Ontario, October 21, 1976. It is written to the President of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation in Ottawa. It reads as follows:
My wife and I would like to voice the strongest objection to the program on nuclear energy broadcast by CBC on "Concern" 8:00 to 9:00 p.m., Wednesday, October 20, 1976. This program made absolutely no attempt to moderate the extreme anti-nuclear positions of the people interviewed and no attempt to present a balanced view of this issue. The people doing the talking were, almost to a man, the most clamorous anti-nuclear crowd that one could assemble. What is CBC trying to do? Are you attempting to turn the public against the Canadian nuclear program, if so to what purpose? That program is one of the outstanding achievements of Canadian science and technology, one that has already saved Ontario hydro some 70 million barrels of oil and will go on doing so. It is quite clearly the best reactor system in the world.
Why is it that those anti-nuclear people and CBC people who apparently have swallowed their line think they have a corner on morality and level headedness? We have noticed that anti-nuclear types never speak out against nuclear weapons; one would think this ought to be central to their concern.
This is not the first time that we have detected anti-nuclear bias in CBC programming. We would like to suggest, sir, you look into it; Canada is being done a great disservice by it. Less attention to sensationalism and inflammatory presentation and more attention to transmitting real information and balanced viewpoint would be appreciated.
Mr. Speaker, it is ten o'clock.

subtopic: INDUSTRY-EFFECT ON SMALL BUSINESSES OF QUEBEC WHITE PAPER ON LANGUAGE POLICY-GOVERNMENT ACTION
INDUSTRY-EFFECT ON SMALL BUSINESSES OF QUEBEC WHITE PAPER ON LANGUAGE POLICY-GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on April 4, prior to the Easter recess, I put a question to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Chretien) concerning the province of Quebec white paper on language policy. I mentioned that many businessmen were of the opinion that the coercive policies of the Pequiste government might have little effect on multinational corporations but could have a major impact on small business.

April 18, 1977
Adjournment Debate
1 asked the minister whether he was considering any special measures in an attempt to prop up the already flagging economy in the industrial and commercial sectors in the province of Quebec. The minister answered by saying that if the kind of policy enunciated in the white paper on language policy were to materialize, some areas of the Quebec economy would be hurt to a considerable extent. The minister went on to say, however, that it is too early to make a definite judgment as it is only a white paper and we do not know yet the kind of legislation which will be passed by the government of Quebec.
When I mentioned that there would be relatively little effect on multinational corporations, it was not to imply that there would be little effect in Quebec itself. Rather, 1 was stating that the large corporations are not only better equipped with staff and have more money to tackle the problems of employee language, literature translation, labelling, advertising, etc., but that they can transfer all or part of their operation without seriously affecting their sales. This is equally true of Canadian companies operating in two or more provinces.
The effect on these large corporations is already becoming apparent. Whilst no major moves are being made, departments and divisions are being relocated at convenient times, and expansion plans have ground to a halt. There may not be a material effect on the profits of these companies, but the loss of jobs to Quebecers who want to stay in their province, plus the loss of purchasing power of those who agree to relocate outside Quebec are already starting to have their effect.
However, of far more serious consequences in the immediate future is the problem of the smaller business which has only one outlet, and that in Quebec. In such cases relocation is generally out of the question. True, some businesses have already announced plans to move. Nevertheless, a company that might have a mortgage on its building, a loan on its plant and inventory, a distribution facility based on local transportation and a regional requirement, has no choice but to try to adjust. With many smaller businesses already in an extremely competitive position, the additional costs to accommodate the Quebec Pequiste government's illogical and ill conceived language measures can effectively put these small businesses into bankruptcy.
The Quebec businessman did a remarkable job adjusting to Bill 22. Very few dispute the need for progressive language legislation, but no one will live in fear of restrictive measures put into force by a government bent on destroying any harmonious relationship that existed between our two founding races in the province of Quebec.
The folly is in the concept that the destruction of an Anglophone run business will provide an opportunity for a Francophone run business. Until separation-which, incidentally, I do not personally fear-and the erection of trade barriers, selling in Quebec can still be carried on from outside Quebec. A person who was not competitive yesterday will not be competitive tomorrow. A bankruptcy in Quebec does not

automatically decrease competition or leave a hole for another new business to fill.
The obvious difference between the federal government's approach in attempting to provide the opportunities by assistance and the Pequiste government's approach to provide opportunities by destruction is readily apparent for all to see. Those who have the choice will not wait to be destroyed.
A secondary effect on the businessman comes from the reduced market. The reduction in construction, and particularly in house building, means less money in the hands of construction men to buy goods, and fewer houses needing furnishings. Once again the large corporation can weather the storm because of its multinational or multiprovincial structure, but when the market goes down for a business whose sales are local by nature, there is no other source of revenue to meet fixed costs, and the situation is likely to deteriorate.
One would not have expected an immediate downturn in the economy following the November 15 election. Business carried on. Houses were finished and the buyers moved in and bought furniture, carpets and draperies. Industrial and commercial construction went on; at least most of it did though there are examples of projects stalled in a half completed state.
It is now that the effect is starting to be felt. Purchasers do not need to buy a new house when there are so many good buys in older and not so old houses. Contracts for new plants are not being signed. Commercial buildings are not starting. Major projects are being re-examined.
Unemployment starts with the construction worker, next comes the equipment and furniture maker, and then the whole economy starts to grind down. This process has already started. The process has been started by the white paper on language policy and will not be easily halted. As the minister responsible for industrial strategy, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce must plan now to attempt to minimize the self-destructing policies of the Pequiste government. Whatever language legislation is introduced, the downturn in the economy is not likely to be arrested.
One Quebec company is experiencing unaccustomed resistance from the Federal Business Development Bank. Another is feeling the adverse effects from programs of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, which is plowing money into a competitor in another province. subtopic: INDUSTRY-EFFECT ON SMALL BUSINESSES OF QUEBEC WHITE PAPER ON LANGUAGE POLICY-GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hope that in the absence of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Chretien) and the parliamentary secretary (Mr. Poulin) the hon. member for Vaudreuil (Mr. Herbert) will allow me to answer his question.
April 18, 1977

The hon. member for Vaudreuil has always been an ardent champion of industrial firms creating employment and contributing to the economic expansion and well-being of Quebecers and Canadians to improve understanding among our French-speaking and English-speaking citizens. I think that his experience and his work in the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs do corroborate what he has said this evening. However it is surely impossible for me in such a short period to comment on all the remarks made by the hon. member for Vaudreuil. The white paper sets as a general rule the right of all Quebecers to work and to be served in French and the charter on the French language will make it compulsory for all Quebec companies having more than 50 employees to operate in French. As for the Frenchifi-cation program as such, it will pursue the following aims: First, make sure that the management and staff of the firm have an adequate knowledge of the French language; second, increase the number of Quebecers who can speak French at every echelon of the firm, including the board of directors. At present, as the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) indicated tonight in his speech in Winnipeg, only 9 per cent of all Canadian firms have Francophone employees at this level, and 43 very important firms in Quebec have no Francophone representative sitting on their boards of directors. Third, prepare a French translation of any working paper used within the firm; fourth, make sure French is used as the language of communication within the firm as well as with customers; fifth, use French in all advertising, except on communication media which use another language.
Through the voice of its president, Mr. James N. Doyle, the Chamber of Commerce of the Province of Quebec has recognized the need to give a more equitable share to French at the higher corporative echelons, including larger corporations. It has recognized also that serious injustice and neglect have occurred, and that these situations must be corrected.
However the president expressed many reservations and made remarks and suggestions to Dr. Camille Faurin, the minister in charge, about granting to public servants the power to cancel the permit of corporations which would take no heed of the new language legislation. This would result in the closing of the corporation and, as the hon. member for Vaudreuil indicated, many losses of jobs, many unemployed in Quebec, and everybody knows we have already plenty of them.
There might be a way to win offenders back without imposing the fines provided for in the legislation. The president of the Chamber of Commerce has asked for a meeting with the minister before the introduction of the bill, to make to him further important representations-

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE-ALLEGATION CATHY CURTIN AND SYLVIA ROCHE TREATED UNFAIRLY AS RESULT OF PROVISION IN FEDERAL COURT ACT

speechtext:
Mir. Elmer M. MacKay (Central Nova): Mr. Speaker, over three weeks ago the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) stated that 18 months prior to that at a provincial attorneys general conference at Halifax, Nova Scotia, he indicated his hope for amendments to the Federal Court Act. The minister made this statement in response to my question relating to a case involving two young Quebec ladies affected by section 41(2) of the Federal Court Act who were dismissed from their positions at the Olympic site in Montreal, ostensibly on the ground of national security. Tonight I just want to have the Minister of Justice elaborate a bit on his answer, and I want to remind him that in my opinion, and in the opinion of a much more distinguished man than myself, the Chief Justice of the Superior Court of Quebec, Jules Deschenes, the present section 41(2) of the Federal Court Act leaves a lot to be desired.
It seems to me that in this day and age we are not giving enough status to the judiciary. We are not receiving the guidance and direction that we should from those distinguished Canadians. In our society the judge is the only official whose only mandate is to do the right thing. Fawyers cannot do it sometimes for reasons of solicitor-client relations, and for political reasons politicians are sometimes not able to do the right thing. The one person who has that mandate is a judge. When a distinguished Canadian of the calibre of the Chief Justice of the Quebec Superior Court is disturbed about the provisions and the use made of a section of the Federal Court Act, I think it is time for many Canadians to be disturbed in the way they were disturbed recently when members of this House brought to the attention of the Minister of Justice the apparent excessive use of the notorious writs of assistance.
Cathy Curtin and Sylvia Roche were dismissed from their jobs, and because of Section 41(2) of the Federal Court Act they had no opportunity to find the reason for their dismissal or the merit of this course of action which affected them so drastically.
Section 41 (2) of the Federal Court Act reads as follows:
When a Minister of the Crown certifies to any court by affidavit that the production or discovery of a document or its contents would be injurious to international relations, national defence or security, or to federal-provincial relations or that it would disclose a confidence of the Queen's Privy Council for Canada, discovery and production shall be refused without any examination of the document by the court.
Chief Justice Deschenes said:
But then, what are we to think of the 1970 amendment to the Law of the Federal Court which sanctioned, in five specific cases, the principle of absolute immunity?
This referred to the tendency of the executive to over-rule the judiciary in proceedings of this type. He went on to say:
Depending on each his own temperament, we may be led to be amazed or smile when we see added, in Canada, the field of federal-provincial relations-
He was referring to federal-provincial relations being excluded. It seems to me that it is rather a perversion of

April 18, 1977
Adjournment Debate
natural justice when a Cabinet minister-and 1 do not wish to impute motives to any of the distinguished members presently occupying such positions in this House-has the privilege or the right to exclude a judge of the Federal Court from the review or consideration of whether evidence ought to be tendered to help a litigant or person defending their position. This is a perversion of the cliche-which is true nevertheless-that justice must not only be done but must be seen to be done.
It is not only the young ladies in question who are affected, but ironically enough it is quite common for members of the RCMP-who are often involved in this type of thing as they were in this case, by virtue of an affidavit of the type referred to, signed by the Solicitor General (Mr. Fox)-to be instructed not to turn over the evidence that would presumably have assisted these young ladies. By a supreme touch of irony, often RCMP personnel themselves, as was the case recently with Gilles Brunet and Don McCleery, get caught in the same unfair situation that we see manifested in the case with which I am dealing.
I do not want to go off on a tangent or cliff-top oration tonight, but I wish to take the opportunity to invite the Minister of Justice or his parliamentary secretary to assure me that this particular section of the Federal Court Act will be looked at and-as I am sure has already been done-the minister will carefully read the decision of Chief Justice Deschenes and look back in the jurisprudence to determine in how many cases people were victimized by having this provision prevent a judge of the Federal Court from assessing whether there was merit in the government's contention that evidence vital to someone's civil rights and legal case would be arbitrarily withheld on the affidavit of a Cabinet minister. It seems to me that this is a very poor principle and that it should be changed.

speakeroldname: Mr. Mike Landers (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE-ALLEGATION CATHY CURTIN AND SYLVIA ROCHE TREATED UNFAIRLY AS RESULT OF PROVISION IN FEDERAL COURT ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the act respecting the Federal Court of Canada was adopted during the 1970-71-72 session, after full discussion by parliament.
Mr. Justice Deschenes recently rendered a judgment concerning the application of Section 41(2) of the act and upheld its legality, after reviewing carefully the Canadian jurisprudence.
The judgment also discusses at length the merits of "absolute" versus "relative" government immunity in relation to executive communications, after reviewing the positions adopted in many countries in which the common law prevails.
Fundamentally the problem is: who shall decide whether an executive communication should be allowed to be withheld from knowledge by persons other than those in the executive branch who are authorized to know of it? Some say that such a decision can logically only be made by those in the executive who are authorized to know; which excludes the judges as well as everybody else. Others contend that judges should be allowed to review the evidence sought and decide whether it should be disclosed or kept privileged. In this latter alternative, in a federal system the further problem arises of determining
[Mr. MacKay-l
which judges should be allowed to examine such communications, whether all provincial judges or commissioners holding subpoena powers as well as federal ones, or merely the latter.
These are a few of the important questions that arise when dealing with executive privilege in Canada, and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) has already indicated that he is reviewing the Federal Court Act. He is studying carefully the judgment of Mr. Justice Deschenes as part of this review.

subtopic: AIRPORTS-SETTLEMENT OF LAWSUITS CONNECTED WITH CAR RENTAL CONCESSIONS-REQUEST FOR REPORT
AIRPORTS-SETTLEMENT OF LAWSUITS CONNECTED WITH CAR RENTAL CONCESSIONS-REQUEST FOR REPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the occasion that brings me here this evening to join with the distinguished Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Roy) arises out of a confusion that appears to be growing around the present policy of the government with regard to rental concessions at Canadian airports. The hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski), myself and other members have posed a number of questions in this House, going back to late last fall, with respect to these difficulties. About two weeks ago, I believe it was April 7, I had a telephone communication with the minister's office.
As reported at page 4471 of Hansard, the minister stated:
Mr. Speaker, those documents are fully available to any hon. member who would want to see them.
The documents pertain to the situation with respect to policy and guidelines for car rental concessions, and in this particular case the formula under which certain concessions were awarded. Specifically, they have to do with why there was a divergence from the normal policy. In the awarding of contracts, why did the ministerial support staff see fit to prepare their own guidelines to meet specific situations?
In response to a telephone call I made this morning, I was forwarded a letter signed by, I am sure, a very sincere and proper person in the minister's office. However, it dealt only with the situation concerning Tilden and Avis. We already know about that because it has been widely reported in the press.
What we have been asking for are explanations of specific inconsistencies going back to last fall with regard to policy and guidelines and their application with regard to the recent awarding of car rental concessions at airports. For example, we want specifics on the inconsistency in the application of the guideline policy with respect to Ottawa Ford-Rent-a-Truck, the "compact" situation, and others. I am sure the parliamentary secretary is aware that this poses serious problems. What we want to know is why we are not to be given the opportunity to see these documents and to hear the explanations with respect to these inconsistencies.
We want to know where we stand, for example, with Host which is suing for $4 million, with Hertz, which is suing for $5 million, and Holiday for $10 million-in all, $19 million. It is not enough for the minister to say to me that I ought not to be
April 18, 1977

concerned with these figures because they are not important. A reference to page 4471 of Hansard will give hon. members an indication with respect to this. I think it is serious. The amount involved is $19 million. We want to know what this will cost the Canadian taxpayer and what the policy is at this point in time.
Is there a policy, are there clear guidelines, covering those who seek concessions? If so, can we be given assurances that these guidelines will be strictly followed? The essence of my concern is this: I do not want to see the Department of Transport falling into the same trap with respect to other rental concessions as it fell into in the infamy of the Sky Shops affair, for example. We do not want the Canadian public to lose confidence in our capacity to deal with these things. I speak in the institutional sense, in a third person sense, because even though I am a member of the opposition I do feel some responsibility for the official management of Canadian institutions such as airports, particularly with respect to the guidelines and policy we follow, policies which do affect the business community.
Perhaps the parliamentary secretary would be kind enough to address himself to the particular document to which I referred. The question remains: which are these documents which, in effect, explain the inconsistencies? Do we have a policy on which the business community can rely, and where do we stand at the present time with respect to the $19 million suits which are-and I quote the minister-being defended at this point? Do we face other settlements? For example, do we face the possibility of the reopening of the Avis case? Avis, I see, was paid $143,000 out of court, $5,000 of which was to meet legal fees. I do not have the figures of the exact amount of settlement in the Tilden case. Do we face a situation in which these two companies might come back and say, "In the light of the circumstances, we were gypped"? Finally, do we now have in place clear guidelines which are not likely to be
Adjournment Debate
frustrated by inconsistency and ad hoc patching up of difficulties?

speakeroldname: Mr. Marcel Roy (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: AIRPORTS-SETTLEMENT OF LAWSUITS CONNECTED WITH CAR RENTAL CONCESSIONS-REQUEST FOR REPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for this opportunity to put on record the status of settlements for damages brought about by the final ranking of accepted tenders in respect of the choice of counters and parking spaces for the operation of car rental concessions at nine major international airports in Canada. To date, Transport has successfully concluded settlements with Avis Transport (Canada) Limited and Tilden Rent-A-Car System which compensate the companies for losses attributable to changes in their original contracts.
A review of the facts will explain the government's rationale for paying damages to these companies. Initially, on October 21, 1976, Avis was informed by DOT officials that its tender was accepted and that it ranked fourth, while Tilden was informed that it ranked fifth. On November 11, 1976, Tilden instituted action in the Federal Court claiming it ought to have ranked third instead of fifth. Subsequently, Avis initiated a motion in the Court to be permitted to intervene in the action. Department of Justice counsel was asked to consider the relevant facts and to advise the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) whether Tilden could have been ranked fourth and Avis fifth. Justice counsel so advised the minister, and then with his approval proceeded to negotiate with the two companies concerning compensation for loss, if any, reasonably attributable to changes in the existing contracts.
With respect to other claims for damages by other car rental concessions, I can only confirm that negotiations are taking place but I have no further details to report this evening as I would not like to prejudice the final outcome. However, as the minister stated in the House on March 30, the hon. member should not attach any importance to the actual figures being used in terms of total claims by car rental firms.
Motion agreed to and the House adjourned at 10.27 p.m.
